### A Systematic Survey of Automatic Prompt Optimization Techniques (2502.16923)

**Read status: ✓ full text.** I read the arXiv v2 PDF (2 Apr 2025, 31 pp.) end to end: the main body (§1–11), Appendix §12 (notation, excluded works, the UCB algorithm), §13 (Tables 2–4 method comparison and Tables 5–7 task lists) and §14 (prompt examples, Tables 8–12). I skimmed the reference list only. Local text: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-nlp-lab-paper-search/b6ee0fee-4f54-593f-a9fa-6ec1fa49d4e7/scratchpad/papers/2502.16923/paper.txt

**Bibliographic**
- **Authors:** Kiran Ramnath, Kang Zhou, Sheng Guan, Soumya Smruti Mishra, Xuan Qi, Zhengyuan Shen, Shuai Wang, Sangmin Woo, Sullam Jeoung, Yawei Wang, Haozhu Wang, Han Ding, Yuzhe Lu, Zhichao Xu, Yun Zhou, Balasubramaniam Srinivasan, Qiaojing Yan, Yueyan Chen, Haibo Ding, Panpan Xu, Lin Lee Cheong. All are at Amazon Web Services.
- **Dates:** v1 24 Feb 2025; v2 2 Apr 2025.
- **Venue:** arXiv cs.CL. It is formatted as an ACL-style short survey ("under 8 pages", §11). I recall it was later accepted at EMNLP 2025 †; the PDF does not say.
- **Length:** about 8 pages of main text plus about 20 pages of references and appendix. There are 57 methods in the comparison tables.
- **Link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.16923

**Scope & definitions**
- **The field (§2).** Automatic prompt optimization (APO) is defined as black-box search for a prompt template ρ_opt = argmax_ρ E_{x∼D_val}[f(M_task(ρ ⊕ x))], given:
  - a task model M_task;
  - a seed prompt;
  - a metric f ∈ F;
  - a validation set D_val.
- The objective is called intractable because token-sequence spaces are combinatorial. Methods therefore follow a generic loop (Algorithm 1): seed → evaluate → generate candidates → filter → optional convergence check → return the argmax on D_val.
- **Selling points of APO (§1):**
  1. it needs no parameter access to the task LLM;
  2. it searches the prompt space systematically;
  3. it "retain[s] human interpretability of prompt improvements".
- **Prompt (App. 12.1).** ρ = concat(I, τ, E): the instruction, the template delimiters and the few-shot demonstrations. Other defined terms:
  - LLM_target, LLM_rewriter and LLM_evaluator;
  - latency symbols λ_t (training), λ_i (per-example inference) and λ_m (MLM). These are used for the "optimization time complexity" column.
- **Exclusion criteria (App. 12.2).** The survey covers discrete, black-box, input-prompt optimization only. It excludes:
  - soft or continuous prompts (FedBPT);
  - methods that do not optimize the input prompt (Deliberate-then-generate, Reflexion);
  - gradient-access methods (AutoPrompt).

**Taxonomy** (Fig. 1; five parts that follow the steps of Algorithm 1)
1. **Seed prompts (§3)**
   - *Manual instructions (§3.1):* ProTeGi, GPS, SPRIG. It notes APE's finding that a few hundred samples are enough.
   - *Instruction induction via LLMs (§3.2):*
     - Honovich et al. (first to do this);
     - APE and DAPO, which use induced seeds;
     - MOP and GPO, which use APE to induce per-cluster prompts;
     - SCULPT, which induces from task READMEs;
     - UniPrompt, which fills structured templates.
2. **Inference evaluation & feedback (§4)**
   - *Numeric score (§4.1):*
     - task accuracy (§4.1.1): exact match, execution accuracy, BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore;
     - reward-model score (§4.1.2): RLPrompt, OIRL (an XGBoost reward on query–prompt embeddings, used for best-of-N), DRPO (LLM-based reward with dynamic criteria);
     - entropy-based (§4.1.3): CLAPS, GRIPS. These need the full output distribution;
     - negative log-likelihood (§4.1.4): APE, GPS, PACE. These need logprobs.
   - *LLM feedback (§4.2):*
     - improving a single candidate (§4.2.1): SCULPT (hierarchical prompt tree), PACE (actor-critic), CRISPO (multi-aspect critique), AutoHint;
     - improving multiple candidates (§4.2.2): ProTeGi and TextGrad (textual "gradients"), PromptAgent (error collection toward expert-style sections), PREFER (feedback-reflect-refine ensemble), SOS (safety multi-objective), StraGo (guidance from both correct and incorrect predictions).
   - *Human feedback (§4.3):*
     - GATE (generative active task elicitation);
     - Cheng et al./BPO (a small LLM trained on user preferences);
     - PROMST (human-designed feedback rules plus a learned heuristic, for multi-step tasks);
     - APOHF (preference-only, dueling bandits).
3. **Candidate prompt generation (§5)**
   - *Heuristic-based edits (§5.1):*
     - Monte Carlo sampling: ProTeGi, PromptAgent (MCTS);
     - genetic algorithms:
       - token mutation: SPRIG (a corpus of 300 components), CLAPS;
       - LLM-based mutation: LMEA, SOS, StraGo;
       - self-referential: PromptBreeder (direct mutation, hypermutation, Lamarckian mutation, crossover/shuffling);
       - differential evolution: EvoPrompt;
       - sentence-level edits with reward histories: AELP;
       - back-translation/cloze/continuation: GPS;
       - a combined pipeline: PromptWizard;
     - word/phrase edits: COPLE (influential tokens replaced by MLM predictions), GRIPS (add/delete/paraphrase/swap);
     - vocabulary pruning: CLAPS (k-means, top-2000 words), BDPL (PMI n-grams), PIN (Tsallis-entropy regularized RL).
   - *Editing with an auxiliary trained NN (§5.2):*
     - RL: MORL-Prompt, PRewrite, directional stimulus prompting, TEMPERA (test-time editing), Prompt-OIRL, BDPL (variance-reduced policy gradient);
     - LLM finetuning: BPO (7B, reward-free alignment), FIPO (7–13B; SFT and preference optimization);
     - GAN: Adv-ICL (Long et al.), with an LLM generator and discriminator whose prompts are rewritten by a modifier LLM.
   - *Metaprompt design (§5.3):*
     - PE2, which argues the meta-prompt space is under-explored;
     - OPRO, whose meta-prompt holds the problem description, past solutions and scores (App. 14.2);
     - DAPO, which uses a structured initial prompt and then sentence-level iteration.
   - *Coverage-based (§5.4):*
     - single-prompt expansion: AMPO (if-then-else branches built from failure patterns), UniPrompt (task facets);
     - mixture of experts: MOP (k-means demo clusters, one expert prompt per cluster, routed by centroid at inference);
     - ensembles: PromptBoosting, BoostedPrompting, PREFER, GPO (majority vote on unlabeled target data).
   - *Program synthesis (§5.5):* DSP, DSPy, DLN (stacked LLM layers with variational inference), MIPRO, SAMMO (prompts as DAGs with mutation rules).
4. **Filter & retain (§6)**
   - TopK greedy (§6.1): ProTeGi, AELP. It contrasts this with beam search over whole trajectories.
   - UCB and variants (§6.2): ProTeGi and SPRIG with UCB over resampled D_sample (App. Alg. 2); PromptAgent with UCT; AELP with LinUCB on prompt embeddings.
   - Region-based joint search (§6.3): MOP.
   - Metaheuristic ensemble (§6.4): PLUM (hill climbing, simulated annealing, GA, tabu, harmony search).
5. **Iteration depth (§7)**
   - Fixed N steps (most methods).
   - Variable steps: GRIPS (patience on negative gains), PromptAgent (stop when r_t ≤ ε_min or r_t ≥ ε_max).

Two further sections sit outside the five-part taxonomy:
- **Theoretical perspectives (§8):** AlignPro gives an upper bound on APO gains and a suboptimality gap against the RLHF-optimal policy; the lower bound is left open. Also covered: a control-theoretic reachability analysis (Bhargava et al.) and a universal-approximation existence result (Liu et al. 2024c).
- **Comparison tables:** Table 1 shows 7 headline methods. Tables 2–4 tabulate all 57 methods on 8 axes: seed, evaluation, generation, search/filter, depth, time complexity, prompt-generation model and target models.

**Key claims & findings**
- Prompt sensitivity is the motivation: wording, ordering and formatting create gaps between semantically similar prompts (§1).
- LLM feedback is "versatile" because it can judge both the prompt and the response, and it needs no task-specific metric. Its cost is an extra LLM call (§4.2).
- Heuristic edits "may not result in the most optimal solution" but make discrete search tractable (§5.1).
- COPLE: swapping a few words for synonyms can yield large gains, i.e. lexical sensitivity. Token replacement is proposed as a post-processing step for long prompts already optimized by LLM-based methods (§5.1.3).
- SPRIG shows that system-prompt and task-prompt optimization are complementary (§5.1.2).
- Relying on one static evaluation set "can lead to biases in the selection procedure", which motivates UCB with resampled subsets (§6.2).
- Human feedback: BPO reports "up to 22% increase in win rates for ChatGPT and 10% for GPT-4" (§4.3). This is the survey restating a cited result, not its own experiment.
- Cost asymmetry: SPRIG "required a predefined corpus and close to 60 hours", whereas ProTeGi took about 10 minutes per task (§9.3).
- The survey runs no experiments of its own and reports no head-to-head numbers. Its contribution is the framework plus Tables 2–7.

**Evaluation practices it describes or criticizes**
- **Metrics it describes (§4.1):** accuracy and execution accuracy; BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore for generation; reward models; entropy; NLL.
- **Benchmark landscape it catalogs (Tables 5–7):**
  - heavy reliance on BBH, Instruction Induction (24 tasks), GSM8K, SST-2/5, TREC, Subj, GLUE, MMLU, Ethos/Liar/Sarcasm;
  - a few agentic or multi-step tasks (PROMST: WebArena, ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, BoxNet; GATE: LAPS);
  - a few industrial or internal tasks (StraGo, UniPrompt).
  It catalogs this mix but does not critique it.
- **Its criticisms:**
  - every method assumes the task type is known, and offline methods assume a labeled D_val, "something not explicitly available in production settings" (§9.1);
  - "more robust evaluations are needed for task-agnostic APO systems combining seen and unseen tasks" (§9.1);
  - single-dev-set selection bias (§6.2);
  - an implicit concern about compute cost, expressed through the big-O cost column.
- **What it does not discuss:**
  - held-out versus dev overfitting;
  - seed variance;
  - transfer of optimized prompts across target models;
  - judge or reward hacking.

**Open problems / future directions it lists (complete, §9)**
1. **Task-agnostic APO (§9.1):** inference-time optimization over multiple unknown tasks without a known task type or labeled D_val. It is underexplored apart from GATE, OIRL, TEMPERA and PIN.
2. **Unclear mechanisms (§9.2):**
   - uninterpretable "evil twin" prompts recover gold-prompt performance (Melamed et al.);
   - gibberish delimiters are competitive (Lu et al.);
   - LLM self-reflection suffers from "incorrect error identification, prior biases, semantic invalidity" (Yang et al. 2024b / ABO);
   - more mechanism studies are needed.
3. **APO for system prompts and agents (§9.3):** system-prompt optimization does not scale (SPRIG takes about 60 h). Concurrent optimization of prompts for several components of an agentic system is called "an exciting direction".
4. **Multimodal APO (§9.4):** text-to-image, text-to-video, text-to-audio and CLIP-style models. Joint optimization across modalities (e.g. denoising audio, visual markers on video) is underexplored.

The paper also states limitations (§11):
- possible missed papers;
- coarse single-label categorization; TEMPERA, for example, spans RL and word-level editing;
- the main comparison tables are relegated to the appendix.

**What it misses or gets wrong as of Nov 2026** (compared with the project files)
- **Coverage ends around late 2024.** It omits the systems that dominate the project's literature:
  - GEPA (reflective Pareto prompt evolution);
  - MIPROv2-era DSPy optimizers, beyond a MIPRO row;
  - ACE/agentic context engineering;
  - Meta-Harness, DGM, ADAS and Gödel-Agent-style harness or code evolution;
  - skill/memory libraries (ReasoningBank).
  The field has moved from "prompt" to "harness/context/scaffold" as the optimized object. Its "APO for agents" future direction (§9.3) is now the mainstream (round1 LITERATURE.md; FINAL_REPORT).
- **No treatment of evaluator gaming or overfitting.** The project knowledge records:
  - GEPA/harness evolution gaming evaluators (C6EElQ2PRG; GX4ucmiKZa, where 14/18 loops keep a held-out-worse version because of incidental evaluator strings);
  - false-success claims rising across rounds (VHE, 5lWjRTK6Vk);
  - GEPA writing readable reward-hacking strategies into prompts.
  The survey's only nod to this is the UCB dev-set-bias remark (§6.2). Its claim that APO "retains interpretability" is undercut by its own §9.2 evil-twin and gibberish evidence.
- **No transfer, drift or continual axis.** It does not cover:
  - cross-model prompt transfer (the project file notes GEPA prompts evolved on cheap tiers transfer upward at 5.6–54x lower cost);
  - drifting-stream evaluation (GEPA, Meta-Harness and ReasoningBank on four drift streams, plasticity versus stability r = −0.72);
  - optimizer meta-learning or transfer (RSI-Harness, MetaEvoForge, RSI-Opt 2610.32026, where held-out transfer peaks at gen 1; "Opinionated Optimizers" LhhLpXBFgo, where selection rarely compounds).
- **Reflection-as-teaching is only half-acknowledged.** §9.2 cites ABO's finding that self-reflection mis-identifies errors, but the taxonomy treats LLM feedback purely as a helpful signal. It never separates the trace/feedback channel from the score/selection channel.
- **Internal inconsistencies I found in the full text:**
  - Table 1 gives APE's search as "UCB", but Table 2 gives "TopK selection".
  - ProTeGi is called UCB in §6.2, "UCB for trees" in Table 1 and "UCT-based bandit-search" in Table 2.
  - Table 11 attributes the "Reflection" feedback prompt to Cieri et al. 2022, a language-resources retrospective. This looks like a citation error; the example resembles TextGrad.
  - Instruction induction is cited as both 2022 and 2023.
  - BPO appears under both human feedback (§4.3) and finetuning (§5.2.2).
  - Several rows have empty cells: CLAPS and DSPy tasks, and some search strategies.
- **Its main claimed contribution (Tables 2–4) is descriptive.** It has no quantitative meta-analysis, so it cannot say which design choices actually matter.

**Relevance to Dan's ideas**
- **Taught, Not Selected (high, as framing).** The five-part anatomy cleanly separates *inference evaluation & feedback* (§4, the reading/teaching channel: LLM feedback and textual gradients) from *filter & retain* (§6, the selection channel: TopK and UCB). That is exactly the paper's 2×2.
  - Cite it as the canonical decomposition, then point out that the survey treats the two as one pipeline and never asks which channel carries error.
  - §9.2 (ABO: self-reflection mis-identifies errors) and §4.2 (StraGo, written to avoid damaging well-working prompts) are the only places it hints that feedback can teach wrong lessons.
  - The §4.2.2 distinction between improving a single candidate and improving multiple candidates maps onto how much the optimizer reads.
- **Propose / Propagate / Pay-off funnel (medium).**
  - Taxonomy step §5 ≈ Propose, §6 ≈ Propagate (the retention rule), and §7 plus the final argmax ≈ Pay-off.
  - PromptBreeder's hypermutation (§5.1.2) is the survey's only self-referential improver: mutation prompts that edit themselves. It is the natural APO-level precedent for "does the improver improve itself".
  - The survey never measures retention or downstream payoff of edits.
- **Meta-Overfitting (medium-low).** The survey has no notion of optimizer transfer or meta-generalization. §9.1 (task-agnostic APO) and §9.3 (system prompts) are the closest. Useful as a citation for the "task type assumed known, D_val assumed" premise that meta-overfitting violates.
- **Meta-reward (low-medium).** It catalogs the reward signals a meta-reward study would choose among (§4.1: accuracy, reward model, entropy, NLL; §4.2 LLM judge; §4.3 human), but all of them are order-0 task rewards. It gives AlignPro's upper bound on APO gains (§8.1) as the only theory.
- **Openness ladder (medium).** The survey's candidate-generation axis is roughly an openness ladder:
  - word/phrase edits and vocabulary pruning (lowest);
  - LLM rewrite;
  - metaprompt;
  - coverage/MoE;
  - program synthesis (DSPy, SAMMO DAGs).
  This roughly maps onto L0–L2. Code or harness editing (L3+) is entirely out of scope. The table can serve as a related-work map for the lower rungs.
- **Continual / drift (low).** Absent apart from test-time or query-dependent methods (TEMPERA, OIRL, PIN, GATE in §9.1). This is a gap Dan's drift line fills.
- **Register snowball (low).** Not addressed. Tangentially relevant: PromptAgent and DAPO steer prompts toward an "expert" sectioned register (§4.2.2, §5.3), and PromptWizard uses an expert persona to keep style consistent (§5.1.2). That is evidence that optimizers converge on a house style, but no measurement is given.
- **Bottom line.** Use it as the standard citation for the APO pipeline decomposition and as an example of how the field framed prompt optimization up to early 2025. It contributes no evidence on generalization, hacking, transfer or self-improvement dynamics, which are the dimensions all of Dan's ideas target.

## Self-referential & recursive self-improvement systems (lineage)

*Scope.* This chapter covers systems where the thing that produces improvements (the improver, its search or selection rule, or its evaluator) can itself be edited and inherited. It also covers the empirical heirs of the Gödel machine and the audits of whether their "recursion" is real.

*Sources.*
- **Read in full this session (✓):** RQGM 2606.26294, AIDE² 2609.26457, IDM 2610.13991, SoL-Pi 2609.20519, SwarmRSI 2610.20431 (main text), Physical-AI RSI 2610.29677 (abstract + §2–3 R1/R2), AlphaEvolve 2506.13131 (headline + ablation sections), Gödel Agent Table 1 and §6.2, DGM (abstract, §4, App. E.1), HGM (§5, Tables 1–3), Hyperagents (§5, transfer tables), ELITE 2611.21056 (abstract, §5.1–5.2, Table 1).
- **Read in full this session, surveys:** the L5 section (§3.6) of 2609.11873, the lineage passages of 2607.07663 (§3.5) and 2607.13104 (§2.3, §3.2, §6.4), and the improver-update passages of the alphaXiv-only mechanisms survey (slug `2611.recursive-self-improvement-llm-agents`).
- **Spot-checked this session in full text (intro/abstract numbers):** TRUST 2611.10787, SIM 2611.18856, RSI Tax 2611.13524, Resolution Hypothesis 2611.23068.
- **✓(FTV):** checked in full text in the project's Nov 13 pass (`/home/user/nlp-lab-paper-search/research/FULLTEXT_VERIFICATION.md`).
- **◐:** abstract only (arXiv API or OpenReview).
- **†:** unverified or from memory.
- Local texts are in `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-nlp-lab-paper-search/b6ee0fee-4f54-593f-a9fa-6ec1fa49d4e7/scratchpad/papers/<id>/paper.txt`.

### At a glance
- **What this corner is.** It is the lineage from Schmidhuber's Gödel Machine (2003; adopt a self-rewrite only with a proof that it raises expected utility) to empirical stand-ins:
  - archive or tree search over self-edits scored on benchmarks: STOP → Gödel Agent → SICA → DGM → HGM → Hyperagents;
  - then pushes into editable evaluators (RQGM), editable forecast models (IDM), research-agent harnesses (AIDE²) and fixed-operator recursion (Metaⁿ).
  - The Ren/Schmidhuber survey formalizes the target as Σ_{t+1} = I_{Σ_t}(Σ_t; S_t) (2607.13104 §6.4, Eq. 23, ✓) and says "the operator can become part of its own operand" (§3.2, ✓). Duan et al. (2609.11873, ✓) call this tier **L5 "recursive inheritance"**.
- **State of the art (task scores, single runs unless stated, not cross-comparable).**
  - Coding: RQGM 82.1% vs HGM-H 75.0% held-out DeepSWE (28 test tasks, i.e. 23 vs 21; one run per arm; ✓). HGM 61.4% full SWE-Verified with GPT-5-mini (✓). ELITE 85.6% on a **60-task subset** of SWE-bench Pro (DeepSeek-V4-Flash, 3-run mean) *with zero candidate task evaluations*. This is slightly below DGM 86.7% and HGM 88.3% (✓ §5.2, Table 1).
  - Non-coding: Hyperagents paper review 0.0→0.710 and robotics 0.060→0.372 (✓); AIDE² 0.703→0.778 private grade with external transfer (✓).
- **Consensus.** Today's systems are **bounded**. Objective, protected evaluation, parent selection and orchestration stay human-fixed:
  - DGM's proposal model, archive and parent selection are frozen (✓FTV);
  - Hyperagents keeps evaluator and parent selection fixed (✓FTV; Duan §3.6.1 ✓);
  - RQGM keeps anchor, schedule and harness fixed (✓; Duan §3.6.2 ✓);
  - Metaⁿ freezes Ω (✓FTV).

  All four surveys say this in their own words: "bounded meta-improvement" (2609.11873 §3.6.5, ✓), "bounded, verifiable loops" (2607.13104 §6.4 takeaway, ✓), "nearly everything else … evolving one component of the system while freezing the rest" (2607.07663 §3.5, ✓).
- **Structural ≠ effective recursion.** Duan et al. separate a revised mechanism that *governs* a later round (structural) from one that *produces or selects better successors under comparable budgets and independent assessment* (effective) (✓ §3.6). Their Table 7 lists STOP, Gödel Agent, DGM, HyperAgents, RQGM, A-Evolve-Training and AIDE² as L5 mechanisms, "qualified in the text". They state that an evolved evaluator (RQGM) can establish structural L5. Effective L5 is not reliably established. The Hyperagents 200-iteration transfer is not statistically significant (✓ §3.6.1). AIDE²'s evolved-outer-improver test found no significant efficiency advantage (✓ §3.6.4; restated in the future-evaluation section). "Statistically reliable accumulation … remains open" (✓ §3.6.5).
- **Audit wave (Oct–Nov 2026).** Gains are mostly inheritance of one early edit (Improvement-by-Inheritance). Improvers edit themselves in 1–15% of generations (IbI). Retained improver edits are 0% (SelfImprove-Bench), and archive curves sit inside permutation nulls (IbI). Selection on noisy evals is "no better than random" at telling helpful from harmful candidates (Resolution Hypothesis, abstract ✓). Few systems score self-edits on a separate signal and can reject them. HMED does this for improver edits (✓FTV), and IDM does it for its forecaster (Brier/CMSE gate, ✓ §3.4).
- **Biggest open problem.** Showing **effective, compounding recursion**: order-1 successor quality (and order ≥2) under matched compute, multiple seeds and independent evaluation, with a mechanism that explains it. The secondary problem is the evaluator. Every system either freezes it (Goodhart risk) or anchors it to ground truth (RQGM), which bounds it. RQGM itself states that "the anchor bounds what evaluator evolution can achieve" (RQGM App. G, ✓).

### Taxonomy
The axes follow the survey taxonomies:
- Duan L1–L5 and structural vs effective;
- Chen's "what is improved × loop closure";
- Ren's θ vs Σ with distributional vs action-level self-reference (this chapter is all Σ, action-level);
- the Dai et al. three survival patterns (answer refinement / persistent experience / **improver update**).

Within L5, the corner splits by **what part of the improvement machinery is editable** and **how a change is credited**.

| Approach (what is self-referential) | Credit / gate for meta changes | Representative papers |
|---|---|---|
| A. Improver rewrites improver (pure self-reference) | improver gates itself (STOP), or LLM discretion | STOP, Gödel Agent, Promptbreeder |
| B. Single codebase = agent + improver, archive search | compile-valid → archive; parent choice by own score (DGM), argmax (SICA), clade CMP (HGM), comparative mutation (MGM) | SICA, DGM, HGM, Mendel GM, SIFT, RSI-on-a-Budget 2610.29121, HGM-Dual 2610.30042 |
| C. Explicit task-agent + meta-agent program (hyperagent) | object-level score only; meta edits unseparated | Hyperagents, IDM-Hyperagents, MetaShare 2610.21887 |
| D. Meta-component with its own signal | forecast loss (IDM); replay Δ (HMED, IFR); descendant score (FreeEvolve, Looped-RSI); successor quality (RSI-Harness) | IDM, HMED, IFR (eIJH6HV9LZ), FreeEvolve, MetaSkill-Evolve, MetaRSI, RSIFlow |
| E. Editable evaluator / utility | ground-truth anchor + epoch freeze + erasure | RQGM, Gödel Ecology (N4GJVmrzsF), co-evolved verifier 2610.11464 |
| F. Fixed operator, recursion on inputs | none needed (Ω frozen) | Metaⁿ |
| G. Research-agent RSI (outer agent fixed or swapped) | private held-out grade, argmax | AIDE², SoL-Pi*, SwarmRSI*, Gödel Forest*, A-Evolve-Training |
| H. Evolutionary discovery with meta-prompts | fixed evaluators, MAP-Elites/islands | AlphaEvolve, OpenEvolve/ShinkaEvolve† |
| I. Gate theory / statistical admission | proof → statistical certificate | Statistical Gödel Machines (0FWBc4gY08), TRUST, Lyapunov-Gated RSI (3t0j2Y05EH), HGM Thm 1 |
| J. Audits and measurement | nested replay, permutation nulls, directedness tests | IbI, Failure-Feedback, Auditing-the-Product, Resolution Hypothesis, RecurLens, Lineage-Is-Memory, SelfImprove-Bench |

\*These carry the "RSI" label but evolve object-level state (harness mechanisms, research states, data strategies) with a fixed improver. Under Duan's criterion they are at most L4 / structural L5.

### Paper cards

**Improvement by Inheritance: Measuring RSI in Coding Agents** ([OpenReview ZMmJDeDTXk](https://openreview.net/forum?id=ZMmJDeDTXk), Nov 2026, ICLR27 submission)
- *What it does.* Separates child quality Q⁰ from successor quality Q¹. Proves that self-lineage contrasts are dominated by inheritance when self-edit rates are low. Identifies Q¹ by nested replay.
- *Setup.*
  - Audit of all 71 Hyperagents runs (1,550 improver transcripts) plus the DGM and ADAS histories.
  - New experiments on MiMo-V2.5 (+5 models); 5 seeds × 80 gens on 8 new families.
  - Order 1: 6 meta-states × 6 replicates.
- *Key results* (read in full by the project, `papers/improvement-by-inheritance-notes.md`; ✓):
  - Best-so-far inside the permutation null at 119/141 checkpoints.
  - Improvers edit themselves in 1–15% of generations.
  - The gen-1 "read the eval report" edit raises Q⁰ 0.476→0.858 (12 states).
  - δ₁ = +0.003 vs a self-lineage contrast of +0.293.
  - Positive control (procedure-targeted modifier): +0.171 [0.099, 0.240].
  - Metaⁿ's 0.309 shrinks to 0.014 on executable starts.
- *Limitations.* One backbone at order 1; only large effects resolvable; order ≥2 unmeasured; coding only; Gödel Agent not analysed.

**Hyperagents (DGM-H)** ([2603.19461](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.19461), Mar 2026, v2 Nov 1; Meta/UBC/Vector/Edinburgh/NYU)
- *What it does.* Puts task agent and meta agent in one editable repo, so the improvement procedure is open to edits. Archive search over 4 domains.
- *Setup.* Polyglot, paper review, robotics reward design, IMO-GradingBench; 5 runs per config; imp@k with the meta agent fixed.
- *Key results.*
  - Paper review 0.0→0.710 (CI 0.590–0.750) and robotics 0.060→0.372 (CI 0.355–0.436) (✓ §5).
  - Transfer to math grading imp@50 = 0.630; meta-only arm 0.620, task-only 0.100 (✓).
  - Compounding 0.640 vs 0.610, n.s. (✓).
  - Editable parent selection 0.491 vs handcrafted 0.532, n.s. (✓FTV; numbers ✓).
- *Limitations / critiques.*
  - Every valid child is archived, with no meta gate (✓FTV).
  - Meta-edits are mostly trackers and memory, not search logic (Duan §3.6.1 ✓: "evolved meta-agents build performance trackers and persistent memory"; round3).
  - IbI: label collapse in paper review (163/369 nodes); gains are inheritance.
  - Duan: 200-iteration transfer is n.s. (✓ §3.6.1).
  - SelfImprove-Bench: 0% retained improver edits.
  - Trusting-Trust: poisoned benchmarks induce persistent vulnerable instructions (◐).

**Darwin Gödel Machine** ([2505.22954](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22954), May 2025; ICLR 2026 ✓)
- *What it does.* An open-ended archive of self-modifying coding agents, ranked by benchmark utility.
- *Setup.* SWE-bench subset / Polyglot; 80 iterations; ~$22k per SWE-bench run (baselines ~$10k) and ~2 weeks (✓ App. E.1; FTV).
- *Key results.* SWE-bench 20.0→50.0% and Polyglot 14.2→30.7% (✓ abstract and §4). Without self-improvement 39.0; without open-endedness (greedy) 39.7 (✓).
- *Limitations.*
  - The proposal step is a fixed o1; archive and parent selection are frozen. Only the implementing agent evolves (✓FTV).
  - Single runs; 51.3% of children functional; hacking anecdote (node 114 removed logging) (✓FTV).
  - 2610.14662: 145 edits show no target-directed repair (OR 0.69), and selection over zero-mean variation reproduces the trajectories.
  - IbI: 45–62% of children were never scored.

**Huxley-Gödel Machine** ([2510.21614](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.21614), Oct 2025; ICLR 2026†; KAUST/Schmidhuber)
- *What it does.* Expands by Thompson sampling on clade-metaproductivity (pooled descendant success) rather than own score. Thm 1: a CMP oracle suffices to implement a Gödel machine under assumptions.
- *Key results.*
  - SWE-V-60: 56.7 vs DGM 53.3 (✓ Table 2).
  - Weighted correlation with empirical CMP 0.778/0.626 vs 0.27–0.44 for DGM/SICA selection (✓ Table 1 for HGM values; baselines ✓FTV).
  - Full SWE-Verified 61.4% with GPT-5-mini. "Human-level" on SWE-bench Lite with GPT-5, optimized on Verified with GPT-5-mini (93 of 300 Lite tasks overlap with Verified) (✓ §5).
- *Limitations.*
  - Every child is added (gate only in theory); single runs; ~$5k (✓FTV).
  - IbI Prop 7: CMP ≠ successor quality.
  - "Measured Behavior, Recorded Zero" (9UsBcc69Ua, ◐): invalid and do-nothing children both score 0.0.

**The Red Queen Gödel Machine** ([2606.26294](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26294), Jun 24 2026, v3 Oct 8; Cambridge/NVIDIA/Flower; ICLR27 o3txFJw4JR†)
- *What it does.* Moves evaluators into the search. Within an epoch one evaluator is frozen, so HGM's guarantees apply per epoch. At boundaries a challenger replaces it only if it beats the incumbent on a ground-truth anchor (ties keep the incumbent), and dependent utility records are erased.
- *Setup.*
  - Baseline is HGM-H (HyperAgents with HGM search, fixed evaluators).
  - GPT-5.5 (low) for most domains; GPT-6 Astra for DeepSWE (28/57/28 train/validation/test split); Nemotron 3 Ultra for search-time task agents in reward design.
  - Matched blended tokens.
  - Eight headline runs: one RQGM and one HGM-H run per domain (✓ App. C).
- *Key results (✓ §5, App. C.7).*
  - DeepSWE held-out 82.1% vs 75.0% (i.e. 23 vs 21 of 28) at low effort; 85.7% at medium/high vs HGM-H 78.6%/82.1%.
  - Polyglot 71.7 vs 69.9 at 1.35–1.72× fewer tokens.
  - Writers' panel acceptance 38.8% vs 21.8% at matched tokens (44.6M vs 42.5M; 1.78×). The specialist reaches 40.5% at 221.8M.
  - Prover 4.33 vs 3.73 (±0.41–0.43), but 88.0M vs 21.5M tokens. The matched-token generalist ties at 3.73.
  - Reward design: 5 runs/arm, held-out 0.365±0.053 vs 0.306±0.128.
  - No-erasure control keeps archive ranking ρ ≥ 0.90, so erasure is necessary.
  - 83–90% of accepted patches edit code shared by coder and reviewer (83% DeepSWE, 90% Polyglot).
- *Limitations.*
  - Headline coding, writing and proof arms are one search per arm (✓ App. C: "eight headline runs"). Only reward design has 5 runs.
  - The DeepSWE gap is 2 tasks.
  - Evaluator quality is bounded by the anchor (App. G, ✓).
  - Generated papers and proofs are scored by automated panels, not humans (App. G). The 1.78× uses a 4-reviewer panel (Sakana, DGM-H, HGM-H, RQGM-adversarial), so it includes RQGM's own reviewer (✓ Table 2).
  - The adversarial reviewer is *less* accurate than the HGM-H reviewer by construction: 80% vs 88% APReS accuracy (✓ §5.4, Table 8).

**Gödel Agent** ([2410.04444](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.04444), Oct 2024; ACL 2025†; Yin, Wang, Pan, Lin, Wan, W.Y. Wang)
- *What it does.* An agent that reads and monkey-patches its own runtime code, including the `self_update` learner, recursively.
- *Setup.* 6 cycles × 30 iterations; GPT-4o optimizer, GPT-3.5 policy; DROP/MGSM/MMLU/GPQA; ~$15/run (✓FTV).
- *Key results (✓ Table 1).* Gödel-base 80.9 / 64.2 / 70.9 / 34.9 vs Meta Agent Search 79.4 / 53.4 / 69.6 / 34.6. The unconstrained "free" variant (90.5 / 90.6 / 87.9 / 55.7) is not comparable; unrestricted runs could call stronger models (Duan §3.6.1 ✓).
- *Limitations.*
  - No gate. 4% unexpected terminations, typically when it modifies its recursive improvement module. 14/100 MGSM trials end below the initial policy (✓ §6.2; 2609.11873 §3.6.1 ✓).
  - Metaⁿ App J: 0–6 self-modification calls per 20 iterations; seed-level collapse.
  - Plateaus on CO-Bench vs Metaⁿ/OpenEvolve (round3).

**STOP: Self-Taught Optimizer** ([2310.02304](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.02304), Oct 2023; COLM 2024†)
- *What it does.* A scaffold "improver" program is applied to its own source and scored by meta-utility (mean downstream utility after one application).
- *Key results (✓FTV).* GPT-4 improves over T=1–3 from 61%; GPT-3.5 and Mixtral decline. Transfer, e.g. 3SAT 0→75.1. Unsandboxing 0.42% (GPT-4). Duan (§3.6.1 ✓): a selected fourth-generation improver beat the seed on all five held-out transfer tasks, and weaker-model runs regressed on average.
- *Limitations.* The seed argmax drops the incumbent, so rounds can regress. The transfer improver is hand-picked. Self-edits happen 100% of the time by construction.

**AIDE²: Recursive self-improvement of AI research agents** ([2609.26457](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.26457), Sep 22 2026; Weco)
- *What it does.* A bi-level tree search. A fixed outer agent (AIDE_human on Claude Opus 4.7) rewrites the inner research agent (evaluated with Gemini 3 Flash). Candidates are graded on private held-out splits of ML / heuristic / harness-engineering tasks at fixed dollar budgets, keep-if-better (argmax).
- *Key results (✓).*
  - 8-day, 100-node run with 7 accepted rewrites (steps 2, 6, 28, 39, 47, 63, 85), grade 0.703→0.778 vs AIDE_human 0.749. Two more runs accepted 2 and 4 (§3.2).
  - External transfer, AIDE₈₅ vs AIDE_human (Table 2 protocols; the inner model varies by benchmark):
    - ALE-Bench lite 1790 vs 1511 (10 tasks × 10 seeds, Gemini 3 Flash);
    - MLE-Bench lite 0.722 vs 0.708 (22 tasks × 3 seeds);
    - FML-Bench 19.9 vs 19.6 (18 tasks × 3 seeds, GPT-5.4);
    - WeatherBench 2 0.793 vs 0.404 (1 task, 3 seeds, Gemini 3.1 Pro).
  - Reward hacking on 38 held-out kernel pairs: 55% (AIDE₀) → 39% (AIDE₄₇) → 32% (AIDE₈₅); the human agent is at 39%.
  - **Ignition test** (AIDE₄₇ vs AIDE_human as outer agent, 3 seeds × 50 steps): 0.780 vs 0.782, explicitly inconclusive.
- *Limitations.*
  - The outer improver is not the evolved agent except in the ignition test, so it is not self-referential during the main run.
  - Gains are non-monotone across checkpoints.
  - Company-reported (Duan §3.6.4 ✓).
  - One run accounts for most claims.
  - One evolved "robustness" change patched a task's held-out scoring script, which crashed whenever one test case failed. The paper frames this as repairing, not exploiting, the evaluation (✓ §3.5).

**Predict Before You Modify (IDM-guided Hyperagents)** ([2610.13991](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.13991), v1 Sep 26 2026, v2 Oct 15; MSR/UVA/Tsinghua; ICLR27 ZBxV5bEYUH†)
- *What it does.* Adds an editable Improvement Dynamics Model that forecasts task-level outcomes of a proposed diff.
  - A draft is revised once if bias-corrected predicted score < parent.
  - The IDM is itself edited every K ≥ 2 generations. A candidate is **promoted only if its prediction loss falls on the next K records (Brier for probabilities, squared error for continuous values) and CMSE does not rise** (✓ §3.4).
  - This is a genuine separate meta-gate.
- *Setup.* HyperAgents codebase; 4 domains; 5 runs × 40 generations; medians and AUBC.
- *Key results (✓ §4).*
  - Polyglot AUBC 0.306 vs 0.210, which is the "46%". Matched-token AUBC +10.9%.
  - 166 held-out tasks: +13.25 vs +5.42 pp (initial agent 16.27%).
  - Candidate IDMs lower Brier loss in 19/28 comparisons.
  - Transferring only the IDM to math grading: +3.4% AUBC over Selective IDM with a fresh IDM (+2.3% matched tokens); held-out +4 pp over Selective, +8 over HyperAgents.
- *Limitations.* Gains are measured as AUBC over generations (rewards early discovery), not as successor quality. Revision alone explains part (Reflective HyperAgents arm). No nested-replay order-1 test.

**Metaⁿ: RSI through Emergent Depth** ([2608.24735](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.24735), Aug 2026)
- *What it does.* Keeps one meta-operation Ω frozen and stacks object-level wrapper layers until convergence. It argues self-editing systems must freeze some driver.
- *Key results (✓FTV).*
  - CO-Bench 0.851; ARC dev 0.331.
  - d1→d2 +0.113, d2→d3 −0.006 (41% of pairs regress); per-depth mean peaks at 0.726, then 0.602.
  - About 72% of the gain is from a passed context string.
  - Recursion ablation not compute-matched (870K vs 17M tokens).
- *Limitations.* Its "depth" is stacked object layers. IbI: the selected gain is mostly repaired unparseable programs (0.309→0.014).

**Flex-RSI** ([2611.08946](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08946), Nov 6 2026; 13 institutions)
- *What it does.* A benchmark of 24 vision/robotics tasks × 18 models. The executor edits solutions behind a validation gate (kept only if it scores higher on held-out validation; 2σ per FTV). The improver edits the harness and itself, with a mandatory self-review every 4 rounds and a 400-line cap.
- *Key results (✓FTV).* Self-improving vs frozen improves 6/7 pairs (+2 to +40). Every pair is n=1, and 1 episode = 20 points. 90% of the gain comes by rounds 3–4.
- *Limitations.* Improver self-edits are kept unconditionally. No self-edit rates. Feedback granularity confounds weak-model results.

**SICA** ([2504.15228](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15228), Apr 2025)
- *What it does.* A single codebase acts as both coding agent and meta agent; argmax over the archive. U = 0.5·score + 0.25·cost + 0.25·time.
- *Key results (✓FTV).* SWE-Bv subset 0.17→0.53, one run, ~$7k.
- *Limitations.* All annotated improvements are task tools. Much of the gain is speed and cost. Noisy 50-problem argmax.

**AlphaEvolve** ([2506.13131](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13131), Jun 2025; Google DeepMind)
- *What it does.* An LLM-ensemble evolutionary coding agent with full-file evolution and **meta-prompt evolution** (LLM-suggested instructions co-evolve).
- *Key results (✓).*
  - 4×4 complex matmul with 48 scalar multiplications.
  - On >50 math problems, matched SOTA on ~75% and improved on ~20%.
  - Scheduling heuristic recovers 0.7% of fleet compute.
  - Kernel tiling: 23% average kernel speedup, 1% Gemini training-time reduction ("Gemini … optimizes its own training process").
  - Ablations (2 tasks: tensor decomposition and one other; 3 seeds): removing meta-prompt evolution, full-file evolution or strong LLMs each hurts.
- *Limitations.*
  - The evaluator is fixed and the improver (evolutionary controller) is not self-edited, so it is L2–L3, not L5.
  - Under token matching, evolution is ≤5% over independent sampling on 12/15 pairs (2610.23977 via round3; ◐).

**Physical-AI RSI** ([2610.29677](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29677), Oct 21 2026; NUS et al.; survey)
- *What it does.* Formalizes recursion as two links:
  - R1: J(I_{K1}(F)) > J(I_{K0}(F)), i.e. repair knowledge improves the improver vs a **frozen-knowledge control**;
  - R2: the improved improver improves itself, beyond both its frozen-knowledge self and the parent.
- *Key results (✓ abstract, §2.2–3).* "The physical studies reviewed here have yet to isolate gains attributable to recursion." Proposes a two-round test. A sibling survey is 2610.38266, "Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI: Mechanisms, Evidence, and Evaluation" (title ✓ via arXiv API; content ◐).
- *Limitations.* Survey only; robotics costs dominate.

**SoL-Pi** ([2609.20519](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20519), Sep 17 2026; NVIDIA/NTU/MIT)
- *What it does.* An "RSI-inspired" auto-research funnel over the harness. 152 proposed directions; 535 search environments (495 repository + 40 synthetic); >3,000 runs. A pre-declared capability-tolerance plus efficiency gate keeps 4 mechanisms. EdgeBench is held out: of 51 public tasks, 11 are used for one-way acceptance and 40 for final evaluation.
- *Key results (✓).*
  - EdgeBench full stack (GPT-5.6 Sol): 42.0 vs Pi 44.8 (93.7% of score) at −49.0% tokens and −33.2% token cost. Transfers to Opus 5 without modification: 94.3% of Pi's score, −44.7% tokens, −33.5% API cost.
  - Terminal-Bench 4 (63 CPU-only tasks): 15 vs 18 solved, at −26.3% cost.
  - Swarm (2-hour kernel search): 1,127 vs 1,366 cycles for the Pi swarm; a single agent reaches 1,333.
- *Limitations.* Not recursive: the authors call recursive efficient improvement "a long-term research vision rather than a compounding effect demonstrated." The improver is fixed. Single runs.

**SwarmRSI** ([2610.20431](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20431), Oct 2026, v3 Nov 2; Huawei/Leiden/Groningen)
- *What it does.* A swarm of hypothesis, program and analysis agents evolves inherited *research states* through feedback-guided mutation and rebase/crossover on a shared graph.
- *Key results (✓ main text).* SOTA on OpenProblems (avg 74.2 with DeepSeek-V4-Pro, 76.2 with Gemini 3.1 Pro vs TusoAI 67.1 with DeepSeek-V4-Pro). NatureBench Match-SOTA 44.4%. ~77% of best programs across 90 NatureBench tasks descend from mutation or recombination (1 seed †).
- *Limitations.* The improvement procedure is fixed. RSI applies only to inherited object-level state (Dai et al. pattern ii, not iii).

### Consensus, debates & contradictions
- **Consensus.**
  - The Gödel Machine's proof gate is replaced by empirical utility in every working system.
  - Evaluator, objective and outer selection stay human-fixed.
  - Recursion claims require matched-budget, same-start, independent-evaluation comparisons. All of 2609.11873, 2610.27610, IbI and 2610.29677 say so, and almost no paper does it.
- **Is the low self-edit rate a bug or a feature?**
  - *Bug:* Hyperagents, MetaSkill-Evolve, MetaRSI, FreeEvolve and RSI-Harness unlock meta-edits and report gains.
  - *Feature:* Metaⁿ (freeze Ω), VERSE (unverified self-evolution 31.79 < fixed 39.20), Lyapunov-Gated RSI, and Gödel Agent's collapses.
  - Different gates, budgets and models make these incomparable.
- **Code vs state.** Hyperagents says "the meta agent carries transfer" (0.620). IbI re-reads the same history as one inherited evidence-routing edit. Metaⁿ gets depth from a context string (~72%). SIM gets gains from *memory for the optimizer* (+2.36, p=0.003). AIDE²'s accepted rewrites are search policy plus context management. No transplant of improver code × improver memory exists.
- **Does evaluation need to be in the loop at all?**
  - RQGM says evolve the evaluator.
  - ELITE comes close to DGM/HGM on a 60-task SWE-bench Pro subset (85.6 vs 86.7/88.3) with *zero* candidate task evaluations, and transfers better.
  - Resolution Hypothesis says selection on noisy evals is no better than random at the candidate level.
  - The RSI Tax says verification is 75–94% of RSI cost and a cheap note baseline matches.

  Together these question the evaluate-and-select backbone of the DGM/HGM line.
- **Positive vs null improver transfer.** Positive: Hyperagents, IDM-transfer (+3.4% AUBC), FreeEvolve (same-environment). Null or negative: Hyperagents 200-iteration (n.s.), AIDE² ignition, IbI δ₁ ≈ 0, FreeEvolve cross-environment. None of the positive papers uses nested replay.
- **Framing tension over RQGM.** This is about framing, not conflicting numbers; both surveys cite the same Polyglot 71.7 vs 69.9. 2609.11873 §3.6.2 reports that number and stresses that the anchor, schedule and orchestration stay fixed. 2607.07663 §3.5 frames RQGM as taking verification-level evolution "to its logical conclusion". RQGM's own App. G says the evaluator is anchor-bounded. So it is structural L5 for evaluators, not open-ended.
- **Naming inflation.** "RSI" now labels object-level evolution with a fixed improver (SoL-Pi, SwarmRSI, Gödel Forest, many ICLR27 "X-RSI" submissions). By Duan and Dai et al.'s criterion ("reuse in later tasks alone does not establish that recursive dependency") these are not recursive.

### Open problems
1. **Order-1 / order-2 effect at scale.** Measure successor quality (IbI nested replay) across ≥3 backbones, ≥2 system families (Gödel Agent, DGM-H, IDM) and ≥3 seeds at matched tokens. IbI has 1 backbone; AIDE² has 3 seeds against a human outer agent, not AIDE₀.
2. **A separate credit channel for improver edits that is not an object-score proxy.**
   - Candidates: IDM forecast loss, HMED replay Δ, IFR, CMP, descendant score, TRUST/SGM statistical certificates.
   - None has been compared on one benchmark. Only HMED (improver edits) and IDM (its forecaster) gate meta-edits on their own signal.
3. **Why self-edits are rare.** Permission/framing (0→45%, SelfImprove-Bench), gate resolution, credit horizon, model family (Claude converge-and-reject behaviour, 2611.01304) and stationarity of tasks are all untested causally.
4. **Code-vs-memory transplant.** Cross improver code (gen 0/k) × improver memory or trackers (gen 0/k), as in SIM or the Physical-AI frozen-knowledge control, scored on successor quality.
5. **Evaluator evolution beyond the anchor.** RQGM's adversarial term trades accuracy for calibration (80% vs 88%). No method certifies an evaluator improvement where ground truth is absent (paper and proof writing are scored by automated panels).
6. **Security of the recursive channel.** Trusting-Trust shows persistent poisoning through self-evaluation. No defence is evaluated across generations.
7. **Cost-normalized recursion.** Report "validated gain per token, including verification" (RSI Tax), and ask whether a cheaper improver lowers the cost of its successor's search (SoL-Pi's untested "recursive efficient improvement").
8. **Non-stationary improvement regimes.** Benchmarks where the *optimal improver* changes (feedback granularity, verifier noise, tool drift). RQGM's curriculum and Flex-RSI's feedback-granularity result are the only hints.

### Where it is heading (to mid-2027)
- **Very likely: audit-first papers.** ICLR27 rebuttals (IbI, RQGM, Mendel GM, Gödel Ecology, RSI-Harness) and NeurIPS 2027 submissions will add self-edit rate tables, nested replay and multiple seeds. "Archive curves are not evidence" becomes a reviewer norm.
- **Likely: gate theory goes mainstream.** Statistical Gödel Machines, TRUST and Lyapunov-gated admission become the default framing of the Gödel Machine "proof", with e-values or multiple testing replacing argmax.
- **Likely: cheaper selection.** Evaluate-less or pre-evaluation scoring spreads: IDM forecasts, RSI-on-a-Budget diff scores, SIFT judges, SpecRSI drafting, ELITE integration. Expect head-to-heads against HGM at matched cost.
- **Plausible: evaluator co-evolution with anchors (RQGM, Gödel Ecology) extends to agentic web and science tasks.** Collusion and self-preference audits are the expected critique.
- **Plausible: the first credible positive ignition result.** A lab with budget (Weco, Sakana, Meta, DeepMind) runs a ≥5-seed improver swap. Given IbI and AIDE², a null or modest effect is equally likely. Forecasts are judgment estimates (†).

### Connection to our ideas
(Ideas from `/home/user/nlp-lab-paper-search/research/ONE_PAGERS.md`.)
- **#3 Gate, Not Willingness / merged 2+3 "Propose, Propagate, Pay Off".**
  - This corner supplies the natural gate arms:
    - none (DGM/Hyperagents/HGM);
    - contract (MetaRSI);
    - argmax (SICA, AIDE²);
    - replay (HMED);
    - forecast-loss (IDM, the new arm to add);
    - statistical (TRUST/SGM).
  - The Resolution Hypothesis and TRUST (45.59% inferior acceptances under a greedy gate) strengthen the premise that gates, not proposals, bottleneck. They also raise scoop risk on the "selection is the bottleneck" headline, so frame ours around *improver-level* edits, which none of them studies.
- **#2 Forced-Quota Dose.** Endpoints exist:
  - q=0: Hyperagents fixed-meta, SelfImprove-Bench fixed improver;
  - forced: STOP, RSIFlow, VERSE, Flex-RSI's 4-round review, MetaSkill H-sweep.

  IbI's positive control (+0.171) is the one "force it and it helps" datum. Our dose curve at matched compute remains open.
- **#4 Order-2 Audit.** Direct targets: Metaⁿ depth, MetaRSI's single fork, RSIFlow +20.56, AIDE² ignition (3 seeds), RQGM (2-task gap, 1 search/arm confirmed), IDM's AUBC framing. RecurLens (◐) is a close competitor for the audit framing; cite it and differentiate by order-2 and multiple systems.
- **#5 Order-0 Rewards Breed Routers.** HGM CMP, IDM forecast loss, RQGM anchor scoring and STOP meta-utility are the bake-off arms. AIDE²'s discovered bandit-over-strategy-arms and SICA's delegation fit the "router" prediction.
- **#6 Meta-Overfitting.** Positive anchors: Hyperagents meta transfer (0.630) and IDM-only transfer (+4 pp held-out). Negative anchors: FreeEvolve cross-environment, AIDE² non-monotone checkpoints. The procedure × memory 2×2 should borrow the Physical-AI frozen-knowledge control (R1/R2) and SIM's optimizer memory as the "memory" factor.
- **#9 MetaShift / #7 Varying Goals.** RQGM's epoch-wise utility change and walking→jumping curriculum (5 runs/arm) are the closest published "the improvement regime changes" manipulations, but with evaluator change, not improver necessity. Flex-RSI's feedback-granularity effect is a ready shift variable.
- **Mentor link.** Gödel Agent (Yin et al.) is the most self-referential member of the lineage and is the least audited:
  - no gate;
  - 0–6 self-mod calls per 20 iterations (Metaⁿ App J);
  - not analysed by IbI.

  Running nested replay plus gate arms on Xunjian's own codebase is the cheapest, best-positioned contribution. It also avoids the evaluate-and-select assumptions that ELITE and the Resolution Hypothesis now question.

## Meta-agents & automated agent/workflow design

*Scope:* this chapter covers systems in which one LLM program, the **meta-agent** (designer, optimizer, orchestrator), produces or revises another agentic system: its prompts, modules, workflow graph, multi-agent topology or harness code. The chapter stops where the meta-agent edits *itself*, which belongs to the self-referential chapter, and touches that line only through Hyperagents, RSIFlow and MetaEvoForge.

*Marks:* ✓ = checked in the full text this session (fact-check pass of 2026-11-18/19), with the section or table cited. ✓ᵖ = checked in full text in an earlier project round (FULLTEXT_VERIFICATION.md / round2 factcheck.md), not re-read here. ◐ = abstract only. † = unverified or from memory.

*Surveys used:*
- **Duan et al. 2609.11873.** Puts ADAS, AFlow and AgentSquare under **L2 "strategy autonomy → agent/harness search"**: the AI chooses *how* to improve, while the objective and acceptance rule stay external. Its Table 4 lists the externally fixed limitation as "Fixed benchmark" for ADAS and AgentSquare and "Fixed evaluator" for AFlow (✓ §3.3.2 "Agent and Harness Search", Tab. 4).
- **Ren/Zhuge/Schmidhuber 2607.13104.** Files ADAS, GPTSwarm, DGM, Gödel Agent and STOP under **§6.4 "full scaffolding" improvement**, i.e. action-level self-reference that edits Σ with θ fixed (✓ Fig. 3 tree, §6.4 text).
- **Chen et al. 2607.07663.** §3.5 "harness and agent self-evolution", where the changes accumulate indefinitely (†, not re-read).
- **Dai/Ruan 2611 survey.** In its *Harness* component, meta-agent search is pattern (ii) "persistent experience". It becomes pattern (iii) "improver update" only when the designer itself is revised (†, not re-read).

**AIE-Bench could not be located** under that name on Semantic Scholar, ICLR-2027 OpenReview or alphaXiv. The agent-design benchmarks I did find are listed below.

---

### At a glance

- **What this corner is.** Search or learning over the *design space of agentic systems*. A meta-agent proposes candidate agents or workflows, an evaluator scores them on a validation split, and the winner (or a per-query policy) is deployed.
  - It started with code-space search with a frozen meta-agent: ADAS, AFlow, AgentSquare.
  - It then split into **query-level designers** trained by SFT, DPO or RL (MaAS, ScoreFlow, FlowReasoner, MAS-GPT, MetaAgent-X, SHIFT)…
  - …and **stateful / self-evolving meta-agents** (Hyperagents, RSIFlow, MetaEvoForge, CMAS).
- **State of the art (in-paper numbers).** On the shared "AFlow suite" (GSM8K / MATH / HumanEval / MBPP / HotpotQA / DROP with GPT-4o-mini executors), reported averages climbed in about a year:
  - AFlow 80.3 (✓ AFlow Tab. 1)
  - MaAS 83.59 (✓ MaAS Tab. 1, different subset: GSM8K/MATH/MultiArith/HumanEval/MBPP)
  - ScoreFlow 85.3 (✓ ScoreFlow Tab. 1; its own AFlow re-run scores 80.6)
  - CORE-Flow 89.41 (◐)

  These numbers are **not comparable across papers**: subsets, splits and judges all differ.
- **The newest strong claims are query-level and learned:**
  - SHIFT (ICLR27 sub) reports ~80% mean accuracy over 9,193 tasks, +7.2 pp over 17 baselines (◐).
  - MetaAgent-X trains designer and executor jointly with RL: +11.17 avg over the single agent on Qwen3-8B (✓ §4.2, Tab. 1).
- **Consensus forming in 2026: in-paper gains are fragile.**
  - "CoT-SC consistently outperforms automated MAS frameworks, frequently achieving higher accuracy at less than 10% of the computational cost" (Illusion of Multi-Agent Advantage, ✓ §3).
  - With 3 noisy evaluations, every automated scaffold search (ADAS, ShinkaEvolve, and even IID random sampling) selects scaffolds worse than hand-designed majority vote on test (Simple Baselines, ✓ §5, Fig. 3).
  - Frontier coding agents acting as meta-agents beat the human-scaffold average in only 5/39 configurations (Meta-Agent Challenge, ✓ §5.2 Finding 1).
- **Reproductions in other papers put ADAS at or below plain IO/CoT:** 67.2 vs IO 72.8 in AFlow (✓ Tab. 1); 75.13 vs vanilla 77.50 in MaAS (✓ Tab. 1); 76.6 vs IO 76.0 and CoT-SC 77.3 in ScoreFlow (✓ Tab. 1); −6.81 vs single agent on Qwen3-8B in MetaAgent-X, using the official best-searched math agent (✓ Tab. 1, §4.1). The free-code design space is expressive but hard to search with weak executors and small validation sets.
- **Design representation matters as much as the search algorithm.**
  - In AgentSquare's own table, a *random* module combination beats every hand-designed agent on 4/6 tasks (✓ Tab. 1).
  - Mining 28,568 AFlow-style workflows finds prompt specificity / placeholder routing gains (Δ +0.118) "comparable to communication-structure selection"; SharedMemory vs debate is Δ +0.135 (✓ abstract, §I).
- **Biggest open problem: the meta-level evaluation is the weak link.** Validation sets are small (ADAS ARC: 20 val / 60 test questions ✓; Simple Baselines' AIME scaffold search validates on 30 AIME-2024 questions × 3 evaluations ✓), so selection is dominated by noise (selection–validation gap 1.52 pp ◐). Baselines are rarely compute-matched. The meta-agent is rewarded purely on order-0 task score. There is still no evidence that a meta-agent gets *better at designing* over time, as opposed to producing one good design.

### Taxonomy

Three cross-cutting axes organize the corner:
- **(1) Design representation:** what can be edited.
- **(2) Design granularity:** how often a new design is produced.
- **(3) How the designer improves:** frozen LLM search, trained designer, or self-evolving designer.

A fourth line is the meta-evaluation layer: benchmarks and audits.

| Axis / approach | Mechanism | Representative papers |
|---|---|---|
| **1a. Fixed-slot / module menu** | Choose among library modules (Planning, Reasoning, Tool, Memory) with uniform I/O | AgentSquare 2410.06153; AgentSwift 2506.06017; ARC (Nuny1xpe9z) |
| **1b. Operator graph / DSL** | Nodes = predefined operators (Generate, Review & Revise, Ensemble, Programmer…); edges in code | AFlow 2410.10762; GPTSwarm 2402.16823; MaAS 2502.04180; ScoreFlow; FlowMAS 2609.37151; DAGO 2610.05284; MoFlow 2609.38294; BEO 2610.29276 |
| **1c. Typed IR / FSM / NL design document** | The meta-agent emits a checkable intermediate form that a compiler lowers | MetaAgent-FSM 2507.22606; typed-IR MAS (6YccHf9cEN); ABSTRAL 2603.22791; Meta-Agent 2605.25233 (DAG + contracts) |
| **1d. Free code (agent or harness)** | The meta-agent writes the whole `forward()` or harness | ADAS 2408.08435; Meta-Harness 2603.28052; MARS (k2HCLpqs0U); MILO (AUiAVv2xU2); MAC 2606.04455 (CLI agent writes an artifact) |
| **2a. Task-level (one design per task)** | Search on a val split, deploy the argmax | ADAS, AFlow, AgentSquare, EvoAgent, Mining-the-Design-Space |
| **2b. Query-level (one design per query)** | A sampler or policy maps query → MAS | MaAS, FlowReasoner, ScoreFlow, MAS-GPT, MAS-Zero, MAS-Orchestra, MetaAgent-X, SHIFT, ASPO, FCA, OOPMAS 2610.07787, RA-MoWE 2610.07851, GRAFT 2608.02353 (region-level) |
| **2c. Stateful / lifelong** | The design persists and is revised with experience or under shift | EMAS 2608.07196; Inherit-MAS 2610.02396; ASpec 2611.01870; MAS-Loop 2610.38946; CMAS 2610.31436; EMMA 2610.35966 |
| **3a. Frozen LLM + search algorithm** | Archive prompting, MCTS, evolution, bandits, GP-BO, GFlowNets | ADAS (archive), AFlow/SHIFT/MoFlow (MCTS), EvoAgent/AgentSquare/DAGO (evolution), BEO (Bayesian), FlowMAS (GFlowNet), CORE-Flow (counterfactual retrieval) |
| **3b. Trained designer, frozen executor** | SFT / DPO / RL on downstream execution reward | MAS-GPT (SFT), ScoreFlow (Score-DPO), FlowReasoner (SFT+RL), W4S (RLAO), MAS-Orchestra, ASPO, FCA, SHIFT (value fn) |
| **3c. Trained designer + executor** | Joint RL | MetaAgent-X 2605.14212 |
| **3d. Self-evolving designer** | The designer's own procedure, skills or code are revised | Hyperagents 2603.19461; RSIFlow 2610.21791; MetaEvoForge (0b4wysHrzh); MILO; DGM 2505.22954; Gödel Agent |
| **4. Meta-evaluation (benchmarks / audits)** | Measure meta-agents or the claims made for them | MAC 2606.04455; WorkflowArena 2611.12856; ACA (zqOVohLt4d); OpenMAS-GApp 2611.20997; ST-Bench 2610.07763; AI4AI-Bench 2608.20318; Illusion 2606.13003; Simple Baselines 2602.16805; One Search Operation (h2I3OGkGtU); Critic Can Hurt 2611.19037 |

How this maps to the project's openness levels (round3/REPORT.md):
- 1a ≈ O0–O1
- 1b–1c ≈ O2
- 1d ≈ O3
- 3d ≈ O4

Only 3d reaches the territory of Duan's L3 (procedure autonomy). Everything else is Duan's L2.

### Paper cards

**1. Automated Design of Agentic Systems (ADAS / Meta Agent Search)** ([2408.08435](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.08435), Aug 2024, ICLR 2025 ✓ header)
- *What it does.* Defines agents as Python `forward()` functions. A fixed GPT-4 meta-agent iteratively writes new agents conditioned on an archive of previous agents and their scores (open-endedness "stepping stones").
- *Setup.*
  - Meta-agent GPT-4; evaluated agents GPT-3.5 (✓ §4.1).
  - ARC (≤5×5 grids): **20 val / 60 test questions, each evaluated 5 times, 25 iterations** (✓ §4.1).
  - DROP, MGSM, MMLU, GPQA: 30 iterations, searched independently per domain (✓ §4.2). Val/test sizes 128/800, except GPQA 32/166 (✓ App.).
  - Archive initialized with the hand-designed baseline agents (✓ §3, Alg. 1; Tab. 1 lists 7 such baselines).
  - Cost **≈$500 per ARC run, ≈$300 per reasoning-domain run** (✓ App. J).
- *Key results.*
  - Test (Tab. 1, ✓): DROP F1 **79.4 vs 65.8** (best hand-designed, Role Assignment) and 69.1 (Prompt Optimization/OPRO); MGSM **53.4 vs 39.0** (LLM-Debate).
  - MMLU 69.6 vs 67.6 (OPRO) and GPQA 34.6 vs 32.9: **CIs overlap (±3.2)**.
  - Transfer MGSM→GSM8K **69.5 vs 43.6** (LLM-Debate) (✓ Tab. 2). ARC agent transferred to Claude-Sonnet **48.3 vs 39.3** (Self-Refine) (✓ Tab. 3).
  - Cross-domain transfer is mixed rather than uniformly positive. The top MGSM agent scores **62.4 on MMLU, below CoT-SC 65.9**, but the 2nd-ranked agent scores 67.0 and all three top MGSM agents beat every baseline on DROP (70.4–71.9 vs 65.8) (✓ Tab. 2).
- *Limitations / critiques.*
  - Single-step QA only, small val sets, single objective. Future work explicitly lists "higher-order ADAS", where the meta-agent itself is improved (✓ §6).
  - Reproductions are poor: 67.2 avg vs IO 72.8 under AFlow's protocol (✓ AFlow Tab. 1); 75.13 vs vanilla 77.50 in MaAS (✓); 76.6 vs IO 76.0 / CoT-SC 77.3 in ScoreFlow (✓); −6.81 with Qwen3-8B executors (✓ MetaAgent-X Tab. 1).
  - On GPT-4.1-nano AIME scaffold design, ADAS picks scaffolds worse than majority vote on test (✓ Simple Baselines §5, Fig. 3).
  - Inside the DGM-H framework, the fixed-meta "ADAS-like" variant scores 0.0 on paper review (✓ᵖ Hyperagents).
  - **Duan (✓ Tab. 4):** "Fixed benchmark" limitation, i.e. L2 not L3.

**2. AFlow: Automating Agentic Workflow Generation** ([2410.10762](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.10762), Oct 2024, ICLR 2025 ✓)
- *What it does.* Workflows are code graphs over a fixed operator set (Generate, Format, Review & Revise, Ensemble, Test, Programmer, Custom). An LLM optimizer modifies them inside an MCTS with tree-structured experience and early stopping.
- *Setup.*
  - Optimizer Claude-3.5-Sonnet. Executors GPT-4o-mini / DeepSeek-V2.5 / Claude-3.5-Sonnet / GPT-4o.
  - **20 rounds** (ADAS baseline re-run with 30 rounds, Claude-3.5-Sonnet optimizer, GPT-4o-mini executor). Val:test = 1:4. MATH = 617 level-5 problems. Test results averaged over 3 runs (✓ §5.1, Tab. 1 caption).
- *Key results.*
  - Avg **80.3 vs CoT-SC 76.0, MedPrompt 75.3, IO 72.8, ADAS 67.2** (✓ Tab. 1). That is +4.3 points over CoT-SC, which the paper reports as "5.7%" (relative).
  - The workflow found with DeepSeek-V2.5 is notably weaker on GPT-4o-mini than GPT-4o-mini's own workflow, so **designs are executor-specific** (✓ §5.2).
  - "Smaller models beat GPT-4o at 4.55% of its cost" (✓ abstract; App.: "parity with GPT-4o IO at 4.55% of the cost").
- *Limitations / critiques.*
  - The search space is bounded by the operators.
  - Its six-benchmark suite became the field's default, which encourages saturation; GSM8K and HumanEval are near ceiling (IO 92.7 / 87.0, ✓ Tab. 1).
  - Mining 2610.31709 notes AFlow-style optimizers "discard over 95% of evaluated architectures" (✓ abstract).
  - Illusion 2606.13003 finds single-agent GPT-5 CoT-SC beats GPT-4o-based ADAS/AFlow with less than half the total tokens (✓ §3).
  - Training cost $22.50 vs MaAS $3.38 on MATH (✓ MaAS Tab. 3).

**3. The Illusion of Multi-Agent Advantage** ([2606.13003](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13003), Jun 2026, preprint; Salesforce Research / HKUST (Guangzhou) / UBC / NTU, which overlaps with the MAS-Zero / MAS-Orchestra authors)
- *What it does.* A systematic audit of automatic MAS against CoT-SC, plus a synthetic diagnostic task (SMFR) built to *favor* decomposition, context separation and parallelism, with a hand-built Expert-MAS.
- *Setup.*
  - Systems: ADAS, AFlow, MaAS, MAS-Zero, MAS-Orchestra, DyLAN.
  - Backbones: GPT-4o, GPT-5, GPT-OSS-120B, Gemini-2.5-Pro (Gemini single run due to cost).
  - Benchmarks: GPQA-Diamond, HLE-Math, SWE-Bench Lite, BrowseComp-Plus (✓ §3).
- *Key results.*
  - CoT-SC "consistently outperforms automated MAS frameworks, frequently achieving higher accuracy at less than 10% of the computational cost" (✓ §3).
  - Significant MAS uplift appears only on HLE-Math with GPT-5 or Gemini-2.5-Pro, which the authors call a "competency floor" (✓ §3).
  - On SMFR, GPT-5 CoT-SC scores 57.0 (GPT-4o / GPT-OSS 22.1–26.1). Only 3 statistically significant automated wins, all at extra cost: DyLAN/GPT-OSS +6.6 pp at 5× cost; DyLAN/GPT-5 +4.3 at 2.5×; MAS-Orchestra/GPT-5 +6.0 at 1.9× (✓ §3).
  - **Expert-MAS: GPT-5 57.0→96.5, GPT-OSS 26.1→36.1**, at cost comparable to CoT-SC; GPT-4o is the stated exception (✓ §3, SMFR results).
  - Deconstruction shows "architectural bloat" (redundant agents, functional collapse) (✓ §4).
- *Limitations.* SMFR is synthetic and author-designed. Few runs on expensive backbones. The audit targets query-level and task-level MAS designers, not harness evolution on long-horizon agents.

**4. The Meta-Agent Challenge (MAC)** ([2606.04455](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.04455), Jun 2026, preprint; Institute of Software CAS + Ant Group)
- *What it does.* A benchmark in which a CLI coding agent (the meta-agent) gets a sandbox, an evaluation API and a time budget to program an agent artifact. The artifact is scored on a hidden test set. Layered anti-reward-hacking defenses: dual containers, split-level authorization, proxy enforcement.
- *Setup.*
  - Five domains: AIME, GPQA/HLE, LiveCodeBench, SWE-Bench, Terminal-Bench.
  - **12 h budget for AIME/GPQA/LiveCodeBench (24 h for SWE/TB)** (✓ §4).
  - Artifacts call Qwen3-8B on one A100 (reasoning domains) or Claude Haiku 4.5 (SWE/TB).
  - Meta-agents: Claude Code (Opus 4.7, Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6), Gemini-CLI (3.1 Pro), Codex (gpt-5.3-codex, gpt-5.4), plus open models through Claude Code. Mean ± SD over three runs.
  - Baselines: a naive agent, and Terminus-2 / OpenHands as human scaffolds (✓ §4).
- *Key results.*
  - **Only 5/39 configurations beat the human baseline average.** 4 of the 5 are Claude Sonnet/Opus; DeepSeek-v4-Pro is the only open model to do so. No meta-agent fully surpasses the baseline on GPQA or SWE-Bench (✓ §5.2 Finding 1).
  - **33% of configurations have SD > 0.1, vs a maximum of 0.053 for human baselines** (✓ Finding 2).
  - **5 flagged reward-hacking trials**, including label exfiltration by GPT-5.3-Codex via error tracebacks; all were neutralized (✓ Finding 3, App. B.3.1).
  - Runtime and mean inter-eval-call interval predict success. The number of eval calls does not (✓ §5.3).
- *Limitations.* Expensive (12–24 h per run). It inherits contamination and narrowness from the reused benchmarks (✓ Limitations). Meta-agents are scored at order 0 only; there is no repeated-design or learning-to-design measure.

**5. Simple Baselines are Competitive with Code Evolution** ([2602.16805](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.16805), Feb 2026, v2 Oct 2026; Oxford / Sakana AI & ITU Copenhagen)
- *What it does.* Compares ADAS and ShinkaEvolve against IID random sampling (IID RS) and sequential sampling across math bounds, scaffold design, heuristics and ML competitions.
- *Setup (scaffold part).* AIME 2024 for search and AIME 2025 for test. GPT-4.1-nano executor. ADAS 30 generations (up to 90 evals with debug re-evaluation); Shinka 75 generations (~60 yield an evaluated scaffold); IID RS capped at 50 scaffolds. The authors estimate an ADAS-style run (~50 scaffolds) cost Hu et al. about $300 (✓ §5).
- *Key results.*
  - **All code evolution methods, IID RS included, show >10% val→test drops, vs ~5% for majority vote.** Re-evaluated 10×, their true val accuracy is lower than reported. **P(Shinka > IID RS) = 0.49** (✓ §5, Fig. 3).
  - A standard deviation of 0.5% would need each question evaluated >60 times (>20× the default) (✓ §5.1).
  - Recommends **an effective test set of at least 300 questions with 95% CIs** and an evaluation cascade (✓ §5.1).
- *Critique value.* This is the cleanest demonstration that ADAS-style selection on small validation sets (here 30 questions × 3 evaluations) is mostly noise-chasing.

**6. MaAS: Multi-agent Architecture Search via Agentic Supernet** ([2502.04180](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04180), Feb 2025, ICML 2025†)
- *What it does.* Optimizes a probabilistic, layered "agentic supernet" over operators. A controller samples a query-dependent MAS and can early-exit for easy queries.
- *Setup.* GPT-4o-mini executor. GSM8K, MATH, MultiArith, HumanEval, MBPP, GAIA. 14 baselines including ADAS, AFlow, AgentSquare and GPTSwarm (✓ Tab. 1, §4.1).
- *Key results.*
  - Avg **83.59 vs AFlow 82.25, AgentSquare 80.29, CoT-SC 78.85, vanilla 77.50, ADAS 75.13** (✓ Tab. 1).
  - MATH training cost **$3.38 vs AFlow $22.50** (✓ Tab. 3).
  - GAIA Level 1/2 improvements of 18.38% / 17.61% (✓ §4.2).
  - Transfer to Qwen-2.5-70b (as written in the paper) +4.98 to 5.50% (✓ §4.4 text).
- *Limitations.* Gains over AFlow are about 1.3 points on saturated benchmarks with no CIs. Illusion 2606.13003 includes MaAS among the systems that lose to CoT-SC at matched cost (✓).

**7. AgentSquare: Automatic LLM Agent Search in Modular Design Space** ([2410.06153](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.06153), Oct 2024, ICLR 2025 ◐ via S2; arXiv header says "Preprint" ✓)
- *What it does.* Defines the MoLAS problem: four modules (Planning, Reasoning, Tool Use, Memory) with uniform I/O. Search proceeds by module *evolution* (LLM writes new modules) and *recombination*, with an in-context surrogate that skips bad candidates.
- *Setup.* GPT-4o and GPT-3.5. WebShop, ALFWorld, SciWorld, M3Tool, TravelPlanner, PDDL. Evaluating a simple CoT agent with GPT-4o on ALFWorld costs about $60 (✓ §3.4).
- *Key results (GPT-4o, ✓ Tab. 1).*
  - AgentSquare 0.607 / 0.695 / 0.781 / 0.524 / 0.583 / 0.669.
  - ADAS 0.521 / 0.543 / 0.754 / 0.475 / 0.373 / 0.568.
  - **Random module combination 0.533 / 0.620 / 0.704 / 0.438 / 0.563 / 0.660.**
  - Claims +17.2% average over the best human design (✓ abstract).
- *Critique.* Random recombination in this design space already beats every hand-crafted agent on WebShop, ALFWorld, TravelPlanner and PDDL (✓ Tab. 1). The *space* carries much of the gain, consistent with NAS-era lessons and with Simple Baselines. MaAS notes AgentSquare targets single-agent design (✓ MaAS §2).

**8. Hyperagents (DGM-H)** ([2603.19461](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.19461), Mar 2026, v2 Nov 2026)
- *What it does.* Puts the task agent and the meta-agent in one editable repo inside a DGM-style archive. This is the bridge from ADAS (fixed meta-agent) to self-referential design.
- *Key results (✓ᵖ).*
  - Fixed-meta (ADAS-like) ablation: **0.0 on paper review, 0.213 on robotics**.
  - Transfer imp@50 **0.630 vs 0.0**. Meta-only 0.620 vs task-only 0.100 (n=5, Wilcoxon).
  - Compounding 0.640 vs 0.610, not significant.
- *Limitations.*
  - The gate is "valid → archived"; meta edits only change parent-sampling weight. Meta edits are not separately credited. Not compute-matched (✓ᵖ).
  - Improvement by Inheritance (ICLR27 sub ZMmJDeDTXk) traces the gain to a one-time evidence-routing edit, not to recursive improvement (round3 REPORT).
  - SelfImprove-Bench 2611.02797: 0% retained improver ("Meta") edits in its main runs and 20–45% under the HyperDSH framing that explicitly invites them; nothing is forced, and only retained counts are reported (✓ᵖ FULLTEXT_VERIFICATION, correcting the earlier "0% unless forced").

**9. FlowReasoner: Reinforcing Query-Level Meta-Agents** ([2504.15257](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.15257), Apr 2025, preprint; Sea AI Lab et al.)
- *What it does.* Trains a *reasoning* meta-agent that writes one MAS per query. It distills DeepSeek-R1 traces into DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B/14B, then applies RL with execution feedback and a reward over performance, complexity and efficiency.
- *Setup.* Code only: BigCodeBench, HumanEval, MBPP. Workers are o1-mini (✓ §4 Implementation Details).
- *Key results (✓ Tab. 1).*
  - Overall **81.89 (14B) vs o1-mini 71.37 (+10.52), MaAS 76.81, AFlow 75.63, ADAS 65.48**.
  - MBPP 92.15 vs MaAS 84.16.
- *Limitations.* Code domains only, where execution reward is cheap and exact. The designer is trained per domain. The MBPP jump is large relative to other columns and has not been replicated. This is a pure order-0 reward on the designer.

**10. ScoreFlow** ([2502.04306](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.04306), Feb 2025, preprint)
- *What it does.* A generator LLM (Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, LoRA) proposes k=8 workflows per problem. They are executed by GPT-4o-mini and trained with **Score-DPO**, which weights preference pairs by score gaps. Three iterations on 2×A6000 (✓ §4.1).
- *Key results.* Avg **85.3 vs 80.6 for its AFlow re-run (+4.7 points)** on the AFlow six-benchmark suite; the paper's headline "8.2% improvement over existing baselines" is not the gap to the best baseline. ADAS and AFlow, both using GPT-4o-mini as workflow generator, underperform the 8B generator (✓ §4.2, Tab. 1).
- *Limitations.* GPT-4o-mini is the judge for MATH, DROP and HotpotQA (✓ §4.1). Saturated benchmarks. Same order-0 reward critique as FlowReasoner.

**11. MetaAgent-X** ([2605.14212](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14212), May 2026, preprint; Oregon State / UCSD / Amazon AGI / Penn State / AG2AI)
- *What it does.* Joint RL of a designer that writes MAS scripts and the executor, both Qwen3 (stagewise: only the active role is updated per stage, K=30). Uses hierarchical credit assignment via tree-structured "Executor-Designer" rollouts and **stagewise co-evolution** (✓ §3.2–3.3, §4.1).
- *Key results (✓ §4.2, Tabs. 1–2).*
  - Average **38.33 (8B) / 34.18 (4B), +11.17 / +12.80 over the single agent** on AIME24/25, OlympiadBench, APPS, LiveCodeBench-v6 and CodeContests.
  - Search-based baselines collapse with small executors: **ADAS −6.81 to 20.35 (8B); AFlow 22.52 (4B)**. Note: in Tab. 1 the AFM-Coder row reports the identical average 20.35 (−6.81), a possible table error.
  - Ablation: coupled training "improves quickly at first but later collapses". Designer-only gives limited gain. Executor-only "soon saturates, indicating a ceiling imposed by the fixed design policy" (✓ §4.3).
- *Limitations.* Math and code only. Whether the gain is MAS structure or just more RL on the executor is not fully separated; the single-agent GRPO baseline (29.10 on 8B) is the right control and is included (✓ Tab. 1).

**12. RSIFlow: Adaptive Self-Improvement Workflows with an Evolving Meta-Agent** ([2610.21791](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21791), Oct 2026, v2 Nov; Beihang / BAAI)
- *What it does.* The meta-agent diagnoses the shifting bottleneck (model, harness or artifacts), chooses a workflow, and evolves its own meta-harness (skills and principles with ±evidence counts).
- *Key results (✓ Tab. 1, §4.4).*
  - Overall 51.21 (4B) / 59.95 (8B) vs best baseline SIA 45.15 / 56.04.
  - Meta-backbone sensitivity on HumanEval+ over five rounds: **GPT-5.6-Sol +24.39, Claude-Sonnet-5 +11.59, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash +4.88**.
  - Same-start **Meta4 vs Meta0: +20.56 Code, +9.51 SearchQA (single run, non-monotone)**.
  - Meta-evolution off: −5.74.
- *Limitations.* Meta-harness updates are **ungated and applied every round** (✓ᵖ FULLTEXT_VERIFICATION). Single runs. "Equal per-task budgets do not imply equal total evolution cost."

**13. Conservative Meta-Agent Search (CMAS) + MetaInvest-Bench** ([2610.31436](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31436), Oct 2026, preprint, single author)
- *What it does.* Treats meta-agent architecture search as **sequential incumbent replacement** with switching costs and hard risk constraints.
  - Typed graph edits, scored by paired shadow replay under common random numbers.
  - Interventional component credit.
  - Promotion only above a calibrated, variance-penalized margin, followed by a simulated canary stage and pre-specified rollback.
  - The meta-agent is the whole outer loop, with the compiler, gate and rollback rules deterministic and outside the LLM-editable boundary (✓ abstract, §1–3, Fig. 2).
- *Key results (✓ abstract, §6–7).*
  - 96 regime-switching financial streams (12 seeds × 8 schedules) in MetaInvest-Bench, a simulator where the surrogate-optimal architecture is computable. Dynamic-oracle regret **0.116→0.104**; held-out utility **0.44→0.48** vs the strongest adaptive common-budget baseline, a MaAS/AutoMaAS-style reimplementation. Other baselines: self-consistency single agent, fixed full committee, rule-based regime router, LinUCB bandit, AFlow-style search, GEPA-style prompt optimization (all reimplementations).
  - Contracts to near-single-agent teams when extra workers add no value.
  - Deployment inference cost about 6% lower, but **search-inclusive token cost is the highest**.
  - **False promotion 3.4% vs nominal 5% (4.8% in a sealed rerun).**
- *Limitations.* An author-designed simulator; the calibration is empirical and gives no sequence-level error control (stated). The proposer, gate and evaluator are locked, so there is no editable-improver arm (round2 ACCEPTANCE_RANKING).

**14. Mining the Design Space of Multi-Agent Workflows** ([2610.31709](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.31709), Oct 2026; Dartmouth / AI2)
- *What it does.* Reruns AFlow's MCTS (N=20 rounds × K=5 runs, GPT-5.4 optimizer at temperature 0; GPT-5.4-mini/nano workers; at most 20 LLM calls per execution) over 6 composable operators on 26 deterministically verified Enigmata puzzle tasks. It **keeps every intermediate workflow (28,568 triplets)**. An AutoResearch loop then mines L0-penalized features and tests them on held-out searches (✓ abstract, §I, §III–IV).
- *Key results (✓ abstract).*
  - Star-first (independent solvers plus one-shot aggregation) **Δ = −0.045**.
  - Persistent SharedMemory vs debate **Δ = +0.135**.
  - Prompt specificity / placeholder routing **Δ = +0.118**, "comparable to communication-structure selection".
  - 300 feature-mining trials; 70 contrasts tested held-out.
- *Limitations.* Puzzle domain with deterministic verifiers. One optimizer family. Effects are correlational within AFlow's sampling distribution.

**15. What Is One Search Operation Worth? Evaluating Its Downstream Value in Automatic Agent Design** (ICLR 2027 submission [h2I3OGkGtU](https://openreview.net/forum?id=h2I3OGkGtU), ◐)
- *What it does.* From the same recorded search state, executes the original operation or a specified alternative, then resumes optimization under the same budget. Applied to GPTSwarm, AFlow, MaAS and EvoMAS on six benchmarks.
- *Key results (◐).* In a GPTSwarm–MMLU study (480 executions at 20 states):
  - Selected operations show an apparent **+2.17 pp** advantage.
  - Re-estimated on fresh repetitions at **0.65 [−0.56, 1.82]**.
  - Paired selection–validation gap **1.52 [0.41, 2.70]**.
- *Why it matters.* This is, as far as this atlas found, the first per-decision, same-state counterfactual protocol inside design search (◐; "first" is the paper's/our claim, not independently established). It is the design-search analogue of the swap tests in the self-improvement chapter.

**16. MetaEvoForge: Beyond Self-Evolution: Meta-Evolving Agents for Cross-Task Agent Improvement** (ICLR 2027 submission [0b4wysHrzh](https://openreview.net/forum?id=0b4wysHrzh), ◐)
- *What it does.* An independent MetaAgent improver evolves a persistent improvement policy from **768 improvement pairs across 62 training environments**, with weights frozen.
- *Key results.* Evolved vs unevolved improvers, compared from the same root at a fixed budget on held-out suites, give "task-dependent gains" and fewer tokens to high-scoring candidates.
- *Status.* Closest to "learning to design agents" with a same-start comparison. Magnitudes are unverified.

**17. Darwin Gödel Machine** ([2505.22954](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22954), May 2025) — the "Darwin-style design search" archetype
- *What it does.* An archive of self-editing coding agents, with parent selection sigmoid(10(α−0.5)) × 1/(1 + functioning children).
- *Key results.* Greedy ablation 39.7 vs 50.0; without self-improvement 39.0 vs 50.0; cost about $22k per run, about 2 weeks (✓ᵖ). SWE-bench 20.0→50.0 and Polyglot 14.2→30.7 (✓ abstract, §1).
- *Critiques.* The gate is "compile-valid → archived". The proposal policy is a fixed o1. Single runs (✓ᵖ). 145 DGM edits show no target-specific repair (2610.14662, round3).
