| 2026-10 | **Wrong Votes, Right Gradients** 2610.20898 ✓; Collective Dynamics 2610.37553 ◐; **OPST** 2610.32770 ✓ (Google); **ASCENT** 2610.05303 ✓; R-Quest 2610.04299 ◐; random-reward probe 2610.01066 ◐; zero-data self-play placebo trial 2610.reward-placebo… ◐; MS-TTRL 2610.32234 ◐; SelectTTRL 2610.16104 ◐; Three Regimes 2611.01307 ✓ (posted Oct 31) | Batch-level theory of why majority vote works, and a collective-instability theory of why it collapses. Fully data-free self-training from topic descriptors. Online agent test-time training with self-distillation of verified episodes. Placebo controls become a genre. |
| 2026-11 (1–18) | PC-Dr.DPO 2611.09872 ✓ (§1); TTSP 2611.07367 ✓; Kernel-Law Lock-In 2611.11165 ◐; TRUER 2611.13714 ◐; STONE 2611.18916 ◐; SpeCal 2611.20691 ◐; "LMs Can Rewrite Their Own Weights" 2611.21885 ✓ (§1) | Majority-vote error split into population bias and finite-rollout variation. Self-play focused on a single target with no target verifier. Lock-in is predictable early in training. A small labeled rectifier. Easier self-written stepping stones. Hidden-state spectra. A 27B model edits its own weights *by reasoning* (adjacent to this corner, and uses graded answers). |

### Taxonomy

The corner splits on four axes. The primary axis is the **signal source**, meaning where the correctness information comes from. The others are the **update operator**, the **data regime** and the **fix family** used for consensus failures.

| Axis / approach | Mechanism | Representative papers |
|---|---|---|
| **S1. Intrinsic certainty** | Reward = −entropy, self-certainty, sequence probability, or gradient norm | RENT 2505.22660, EMPO 2504.05812, INTUITOR 2505.19590, RLSC 2506.06395, No Free Lunch 2506.17219, gradient-norm reward 2605.09920, Selective Internal Feedback 2610.21392, PowerFlow 2603.18363 |
| **S2. Ensemble consensus** | Reward = agreement with the group's majority, soft vote or cluster | TTRL 2504.16084, SRT 2505.21444, Co-rewarding 2508.00410, EVOL-RL 2509.15194, CoRE 2608.09324, GMAE 2609.36750, MS-TTRL 2610.32234, TCCA (ICLR'27 Cuk60HQcrN) |
| **S3. Self-judgment / self-verification** | The model (or a co-trained role) judges, ranks or writes rubrics | Self-Rewarding LMs †, Self-rewarding correction 2502.19613, RLSR 2505.08827, CoVerRL 2603.17775, CoVER (ICLR'27 DshkmNnrso), SERPO 2607.26873, score saturation (ICLR'27 yHVcEoxOlW), SRO fragility (ICLR'27 IVFASEtqp6) |
| **S4. Grounded asymmetric verification** | Votes propose, and a cheap checker (code, Lean, environment) disposes | T3RL 2603.02203, JURY-RL 2604.25419, ASCENT 2610.05303 (environment success), TTSP 2611.07367 (interpreter on synthetic tasks), the "external rewards" arm of URLVR 2603.08660 §7 |
| **S5. Self-generated tasks** | The model writes its own problems (see the self-play chapter) | Absolute Zero 2505.03335, R-Zero 2508.05004, R-Quest 2610.04299, OPST 2610.32770, STONE 2611.18916, TTSP 2611.07367 |
| **U1. Scalar RL** (GRPO/PPO/RLOO) | Policy gradient on the pseudo-reward | Most S1/S2 papers |
| **U2. Preference** (DPO) | Majority answer vs minority as a preference pair | PC-Dr.DPO 2611.09872, ScPO (baseline in SRT Table 1) |
| **U3. Label-free self-distillation** | A teacher = the same model conditioned on the consensus, its own solution or stepping stones; dense token targets | U-OPSD 2608.06296, CANON (ICLR'27 LiJUIYVa13), OPST 2610.32770, STONE 2611.18916, ASCENT 2610.05303, RCTS (ICLR'27 OCZ3eKMN9b) |
| **U4. Restricted parameters** | Bias-only or LoRA fast weights | Label-free steering 2609.18587, ASCENT (LoRA) |
| **R1. Transductive TTRL** | Train on the unlabeled test set, then evaluate on it | TTRL, T3RL, SCRL, DDRL, PC-Dr.DPO |
| **R2. Inductive unsupervised RLVR** | Train on an unlabeled train set, evaluate on held-out sets | SRT, URLVR-scale, GMAE, Wrong Votes, INTUITOR |
| **R3. Per-instance test-time scaling** | Adapt per single target problem | TTSP, TRT (no weights) |
| **R4. Online streams** | One pass, persistent updates | ASCENT, PC-Dr.DPO (cache), SERPO (sequential benchmarks), safety-in-mixed-streams (ICLR'27 mjNZLUFK21) |
| **F1. Filter or abstain** | Drop weak-consensus prompts, add negative labels | SCRL 2603.19880, DDRL 2604.21327, SelectTTRL 2610.16104 |
| **F2. Fix the advantage** | Marginalize or debias GRPO normalization | GMAE 2609.36750, DDRL, Three Regimes 2611.01307 |
| **F3. Keep exploration** | Novelty or rare-answer bonus, minority-preserving sampling | EVOL-RL 2509.15194, TTRL-Guard 2605.19444, Three Regimes, Beyond Self-Consensus (ICLR'27 BKfYuZRiix) |
| **F4. Monitor or predict collapse** | Flip rate, Model Collapse Step, kernel-law lock-in, N_c | 2605.19444, 2603.08660 §6, 2611.11165, 2610.37553 |
| **F5. Add a little truth** | A rectifier trained on a small labeled source set | TRUER 2611.13714 |

**A labeling contradiction to know about.** Gao et al. (2507.21046 §5.1) list majority vote under "External" rewards (†, not re-checked in this pass). He et al. (2603.08660 §2) classify it as *intrinsic* (ensemble-based) and reserve "external" for generation–verification asymmetries. This chapter follows He et al.

### Paper cards

**1. TTRL: Test-Time Reinforcement Learning** ([2504.16084](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16084), Apr 2025, NeurIPS 2025 per citing papers †; Tsinghua / Shanghai AI Lab)
- *What it does.* It samples N answers per unlabeled test question, takes the majority answer as the label, gives a 0/1 reward for agreement, and runs GRPO on the test set itself.
- *Setup* (✓ §3.1):
  - Models: Qwen2.5-Math 1.5B/7B, Qwen2.5-7B/32B, Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.x, Mistral-Nemo / Ministral-8B, DeepSeek-Math-7B-Instruct, DeepSeek-R1-LLaMA-8B, Skywork-OR1.
  - Benchmarks: AIME24, AMC, MATH-500, GPQA-D.
  - Training: 64 samples for voting, 32 downsampled for training; cosine LR with peak 5×10⁻⁷ (AdamW); 10/30/80 episodes for MATH-500/AMC/AIME24; max length 3,072 tokens (32,768 for LRMs); 8×A100-80GB.
  - Evaluation: pass@1 from 16 samples (4 for 32k-context runs), temperature 0.6. No seed variance is reported.
- *Key results:*
  - Qwen2.5-Math-7B AIME24 rises from 12.9 to 40.2, and the 4-benchmark average from 31.1 to 54.9. GPQA *drops* from 29.1 to 27.7 (✓ Table 1).
  - Qwen3-8B (non-thinking, 3k context) average rises from 53.8 to 64.5 (✓ Table 1).
  - Mistral-Nemo-Instruct AIME falls from 0.8 to 0 (✓ Table 2).
  - Average after TTRL beats the base model's maj@64 (✓ Fig. 7).
  - "Lucky hit": on AIME24, label accuracy is 37% but reward accuracy is 92%, because wrong answers are scattered (✓ §4.2).
  - Response length falls 44–73% across MATH-500 levels, and gains shrink with difficulty, from +45.4 at L1 to +16.8 at L5 (✓ Table 3).
- *Limitations and critiques:*
  - It is transductive (trains on the evaluation set).
  - The authors name failure modes from bad temperature or batch size and from a lack of prior knowledge (✓ §4.3).
  - Spurious Rewards (2506.10947 ✓ §1) shows that random rewards alone give Qwen2.5-Math-7B +21.4 points on MATH-500. Part of TTRL's +36.7 on that model (46.7 → 83.4, ✓ Table 1) is probably elicitation, not learning from the vote.
  - The Extinction Window paper (2605.19444 ✓) finds the gains are mostly sharpening of problems the model can already solve.

**2. How Far Can Unsupervised RLVR Scale LLM Training?** ([2603.08660](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.08660), Mar 2026, ICLR 2026; Tsinghua, the TTRL group)
- *What it does.* Taxonomy, theory and a large sweep. All intrinsic rewards converge to sharpening the initial distribution. It proposes the **Model Collapse Step** (the step at which reward accuracy drops below 1%) as a cheap predictor of whether a model is trainable with RL.
- *Setup* (✓ §4–6):
  - Qwen3-1.7B-Base on DAPO-17k with five intrinsic rewards.
  - Per-problem study on 25 MATH500 problems.
  - Dataset-size sweep over {32, 128, 512, 2048, 8192, 16384} prompts; 3 seeds only for sizes {32, 128, 512}.
  - 7 models from the OLMo, LLaMA and Qwen families for the predictor.
- *Key results:*
  - Every intrinsic reward shows the same rise-then-fall pattern. Failure types: probability rewards give *length collapse*; entropy rewards give *repetition collapse* (✓ §4.1.2).
  - Single-problem training flips greedy correctness in only 3/25 problems (✓ §4.2.1).
  - ≤128 prompts are stable; ≥512 collapse. DAPO-32 never collapses while DAPO-512 always does, across 3 seeds (✓ §5.1).
  - Training on 32 filtered samples where almost all initial majorities are *wrong* still improves out-of-distribution results without collapse (✓ §5.3, Fig. 9).
  - In the Qwen family, the SFT/distilled variant stays stable while the base drops to near-zero reward accuracy by step 200; in the LLaMA family both collapse, with the base model failing by step 40 (✓ §6.1).
  - Model Collapse Step tracks the ground-truth RLVR gain and uses 5.6× fewer tokens than the GT-gain gold standard (1.19B vs 6.66B tokens across 7 models) (✓ §6.2–6.3, Table 3).
- *Limitations.* The analysis is mostly at 1.7B. The "external reward" escape route (§7) is preliminary.

**3. Can Large Reasoning Models Self-Train? (SRT)** ([2505.21444](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21444), May 2025, v2 Oct 2025 †; CMU, Zanette group)
- *What it does.* Majority-vote RL on *training* sets (inductive), with the self-labeling policy updated at every step.
- *Setup* (✓ §4):
  - Main math models: Qwen2.5-Math-7B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-14B-Base and DeepSeek-Math-7B-Instruct (RLOO; GRPO in an appendix). Qwen3-4B-Base on Reasoning Gym for the curriculum experiments.
  - Training sets: MATH-12K, DAPO, AIME 1983–2023 (and Big-Math-RL-Verified for Llama).
  - Held-out: AIME24/25, AMC, MATH-500.
- *Key results:*
  - Peak mean@32 averaged over AIME24/25 and AMC, Qwen2.5-Math-7B (✓ Table 1):

    | Training set | Base | SFT on majority vote | DPO | ScPO | **SRT** | Ground-truth RL |
    |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
    | DAPO | 0.15 | 0.18 | 0.21 | 0.20 | **0.31** | 0.36 |
    | MATH-12K | 0.15 | 0.18 | 0.23 | 0.20 | **0.32** | 0.33 |

  - Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct rises from 52.6% to nearly 60% average accuracy on held-out MATH-500 (✓ §4.1).
  - A curriculum on synthetic tasks lets the model keep climbing (✓ Fig. 5).
  - **Collapse** (✓ §4.2, Fig. 6–8): self-reward and KL spike together, and outputs become random tokens plus a template answer such as `\boxed{1}`. On MATH-12K this happens after about 1200 RL steps (✓ App. C, Fig. 11).
  - Neither the KL coefficient nor the choice of GRPO vs RLOO prevents collapse. A lower learning rate only delays it. Fewer generations per prompt inject noise into the vote and delay it (✓ Fig. 8 caption).
- *Limitations.* The proposed mitigations (early stopping, curriculum, a fixed teacher) are in App. I, and none removes the core problem. Feedback design is the open problem.

**4. Wrong Votes, Right Gradients: Why Majority-Vote Rewards Track Verifiable RL** ([2610.20898](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20898), Oct 2026; Dartmouth / WashU, the R-Zero group)
- *What it does.* Moves the analysis from the prompt to the batch update. It splits the majority-vote update into shrinkage plus *misdirection*, and shows that misdirection vanishes with batch size when label errors are incoherent across prompts.
- *Setup* (✓ §2):
  - Qwen3-4B-Base on DeepScaleR, B=256, n=16, no KL or entropy term. Gold-reward and majority-vote runs from the same initialization see the same prompts.
  - Gradient sketches on 5 models (Qwen3-1.7B-Base/4B-Base, Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct).
  - 164/256 prompts are "mixed" under the gold reward.
- *Key results* (✓ §1/§3):
  - A prompt's own gradient accounts for less than 1% of the change in that prompt's output.
  - The noise-corrected cosine between the majority-vote and gold updates is 1 within error.
  - Majority-vote errors are as incoherent as a random-reward null.
  - Flipping up to 30% of labels at random leaves the direction intact; a shared-rule flip destroys it (at 31% the shared-rule update points away from gold).
  - Rewards that favor a response *type* on every prompt (frequency, confidence, a learned reward model) fall measurably short.
  - Held-out problems with a wrong majority acquire a correct majority at about 3× the resampling rate (✓ §5).
  - The equivalence is *local*: gold training still ends ahead on held-out majority accuracy.
- *Limitations* (✓ §Limitations): training runs on one model (Qwen3-4B-Base), two runs per reward, and the high-entropy regime is not analyzed.
- *Relevance beyond this corner.* This is the most transferable result here. It gives a testable criterion, error coherence, for when a cheap self-signal can replace a verifier.

**5. Detecting and Mitigating the Correct-Answer Extinction Window in TTRL** ([2605.19444](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.19444), May 2026; Meituan)
- *What it does.* Per-problem tracking of initial vs final label accuracy, and **TTRL-Guard**, which combines flip-rate-aware reward scaling, minority-preserving sampling and risk-conditioned sparse updates.
- *Setup:* the per-problem analysis uses Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen3-4B on AIME25 and MATH-500; the method is evaluated on 4 benchmarks (AIME24, AIME25, AMC, MATH-500) (✓ §1).
- *Key results* (✓ Fig. 1/§1; four of the paper's six categories shown):

  | Problem category | Share |
  |---|---|
  | Stable always-right | 44.5% |
  | Learned (zero-to-one) | 0.7% |
  | Degraded | 21.6% |
  | Always wrong | 26.2% |

  - A correct answer is briefly active and then permanently suppressed, and the damage is irreversible once the vote locks on. Flip rate leads the collapse.
  - TTRL-Guard gives +54% relative over TTRL on AIME 2025, and cuts the degraded fraction on Llama from 60.2% to 28.0% (✓ §1).
- *Limitations.* Small models only. The guard rules are heuristic.

**6. Group-Marginalized Self-Rewarding RL (GMAE)** ([2609.36750](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.36750), Sep 2026; SJTU / Tencent; ICLR'27 submission VczpXmXDmE)
- *What it does.* A response's self-reward depends on which other samples happen to share its group. GMAE marginalizes over possible group contexts to get an expected advantage. Variants wrap TTRL (GMAE0), Co-Reward (GMAE-CR) and SR-TTRL (GMAE-SR).
- *Setup* (✓ §5.1):
  - Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B-Base and Llama3.1-8B-Instruct trained on DAPO-14K for one epoch (GRPO, batch 64, LR 1e-6, G = G′ = 16).
  - 8 benchmarks (MATH500, AMC, AIME24/25/26, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, LiveCodeBench-v6), mean@16.
  - 9 self-rewarding baselines (7 ensemble-based: TTRL, CoVo, SCOPE, Self-Harmony, RESTRAIN, Co-Reward, SR-TTRL; 2 probability-based: Intuitor, EM-RL) plus an RLVR reference.
- *Key results* (✓ Table 1). Average mean@16:

  | Model | Raw | TTRL | Best GMAE | RLVR |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | Qwen3-1.7B-Base | 11.9 | 18.4 | 21.0 | 22.0 |
  | Qwen3-4B-Base | 17.2 | 27.0 | 30.1 | 34.1 |
  | Qwen3-8B-Base | 27.7 | 34.5 | 38.0 | 40.9 |
  | Llama3.1-8B-Instruct | 15.8 | 23.5 | 26.2 | 27.4 |

  - GMAE beats the baselines in 30 of 32 model–benchmark cells, by +2.0–2.8 points over the strongest baseline (✓ §5.2).
  - Intuitor and EM-RL (the confidence rewards) are among the weakest label-free baselines, but not the weakest in every block: CoVo is lowest at 4B (22.9) and 8B (30.1), and SCOPE (15.1) sits below EM-RL at 1.7B (✓ Table 1).
  - Across five rollout-sampling seeds on Qwen3-8B-Base, the standard deviation of mean@16 averaged over benchmarks is 0.48 for GMAE0 versus 0.69 for TTRL (✓ §5.3, Fig. 4).
- *Limitations.* Training is on math only. The gap to RLVR stays about 3–4 points at 4B–8B.

**7. Tool Verification for TTRL (T3RL)** ([2603.02203](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.02203), Mar 2026, v2 Aug 2026; LMU / Stanford)
- *What it does.* Votes are weighted by code-execution verification, which suppresses "false-popular" majorities. The authors frame TTRL as a recursive self-improvement paradigm and T3RL as "verified online data synthesis".
- *Setup* (✓ §5): five 1–4B backbones (Qwen-Math, Qwen2.5, Qwen3, Llama-3.2) on MATH-500, AMC and AIME24, using TTRL's hyperparameters.
- *Key results* (✓ Table 1, §5):
  - Wins 15/15 paired comparisons with TTRL.
  - Qwen3-4B AIME24: 36.4 → 40.0.
  - Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct AIME24: 13.3 → 17.1.
  - Qwen-Math-1.5B average: 45.9 → 48.8.
  - Relative gain grows with difficulty, from +0.2% at L1 to +4.3% at L5.
- *Limitations:*
  - A weak verifier (Qwen-Coder-0.5B) makes things *worse* than plain voting (−1.4 average vs TTRL on Qwen-2.5-0.5B), and gains are small on easy tasks (✓ §6, App. Table 8).
  - TTRL baseline numbers are copied from the original paper "where possible" (✓ Baselines), so the comparisons are not same-seed.
  - Most gains are within one standard deviation on MATH-500 (✓ Table 1 ± values).

**8. On-Policy Self-Training (OPST): Data-Free Self-Improvement** ([2610.32770](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.32770), Oct 2026; Google / Ulm; 84 votes †)
- *What it does.* Seeded only by topic descriptors, the model writes its own question plus privileged reasoning and answer. Filters:
  - Pseudo-verification: the model must reproduce the answer in a fresh context and under paraphrase.
  - Consensus gate: drop problems the student already solves.

  An EMA teacher sees the privileged information, and the student sees only the question. Training is on-policy self-distillation.
- *Setup* (✓ §4): Gemma 4 E2B/E4B, with and without thinking. MMLU, GPQA, GSM8K and HellaSwag in-domain, plus out-of-domain sets. A visual variant for VQAv2/POPE.
- *Key results:*
  - E2B without thinking: MMLU +10.2, GPQA +4.0, HellaSwag +7.5 (✓ Table 1).
  - On identical self-generated data, GRPO rewarding agreement with the generated answer gains only +1.0 average (E2B, no thinking), versus +7.3 for OPST (✓ Table 1).
  - Beats R-Zero by 1.4–5.2 and u-OPSD by 1.0–2.8 points, and recovers 88% of supervised OPSD's gain (+7.3 of +8.3, E2B without thinking) (✓ Table 2, §4).
  - With 75% wrong answers injected (filters off), OPST loses 1.9 points while SFT loses 5.7 (✓ Table 5c).
  - A placebo privileged context from another problem on the same topic gives only +2.7, versus +10.2 (✓ Table 5b).
  - The multi-domain ("All three") run regresses MATH-500 by 4.9 (✓ Table 3).
- *Limitations* (✓): it only amplifies existing knowledge; consistent errors pass pseudo-verification; topic descriptors are hand-chosen; models are small; there is no label-free stopping rule.

**9. Test-Time Self-Play: Scaling without a Verifier (TTSP)** ([2611.07367](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.07367), Nov 5 2026; ETH Zurich / Tufa Labs, Krause group)
- *What it does.* For one hard target problem, a proposer writes related synthetic problems with tests and a reference solution, aimed at the solver's frontier. Both roles (two LoRA adapters on a shared frozen backbone) are trained with GRPO, using execution feedback from a Python interpreter. The target's own verifier is never used in training.
- *Setup* (✓ §4–5):
  - Qwen3-8B.
  - HardLCBv6 = LiveCodeBench-v6 problems with 0 < mean@512 < 0.7, split into MidHard (>0.1) and VeryHard (≤0.1).
  - 7 verifier strengths (v0, v25, v50, v75, public tests, private tests, oracle v⋆), from v0 (accepts everything) to the oracle.
  - Baselines: rejection sampling, functional majority voting, ACE.
- *Key results:*
  - Best method at every verifier strength. In the no-verifier limit, mean@8 improves by 35% absolute (◐ abstract).
  - On VeryHard the gain is approximately zero. Below mean@512 ≈ 0.1, the proposer cannot bootstrap a curriculum that leads back to the target (✓ §5 / Fig. 7).
- *Limitations* (✓): compute is per target and not amortized; proposers can reward-hack; the solver's entropy can collapse. "Without a verifier" means *without a target verifier*, since the interpreter grounds the synthetic tasks.

**10. ASCENT: Online Test-Time Training of Long-Horizon Agents** ([2610.05303](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.05303), Oct 2026; UNSW)
- *What it does.* One pass over a task stream, batch size 1. Each environment-verified trajectory, with invalid-action turns pruned, is given as privileged context to the frozen initial model. That model's hindsight distributions are distilled into persistent LoRA fast weights.
- *Setup* (✓ §5): Qwen3.5-4B/9B on ALFWorld, WebShop and AppWorld. Baselines: offline and online harness methods (MemP, ACE, GEPA, EvoSkill, TextGrad, Trace2Skill, ReasoningBank, A-Mem, MemRL, Dynamic Cheatsheet) and TT-OPSD.
- *Key results* (✓ Table 1, ALFWorld seen stream):

  | Model | Base SR | ASCENT SR | Best other method | Turns, base → ASCENT |
  |---|---|---|---|---|
  | Qwen3.5-4B | 46.4 | 69.5 ±5.6 | 63.6 (online MemP) | 35.1 → 26.3 |
  | Qwen3.5-9B | 55.0 | 77.4 ±1.8 | 69.3 (offline MemP, online ACE) | 32.6 → 21.0 |

  - Naive online imitation, RFT and REINFORCE variants drift and end *below* the base model (✓ §3.2, Fig. 1).
- *Limitations* (✓): needs open weights for full next-token distributions; sparse episode-level gating; equal weighting of turns; the teacher may reconstruct student tokens. It is "label-free" only in that it uses no human labels, since the environment success flag is the verifier.
- *Relevance.* The most direct weights-vs-harness comparison in this chapter.

**11. SERPO: Self-Evolving Rubric Policy Optimization for Open-Ended TTRL** ([2607.26873](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26873), Jul 2026; HUST / USTC / Alibaba †; ICLR'27 npwCnxrO6F)
- *What it does.* Replaces answer voting with three things that evolve together:
  - Good–Normal–Bad response archives;
  - query-specific rubrics that are kept only if they discriminate the archives;
  - a criterion score computed from verdict-token likelihoods.
- *Setup:* Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and Qwen3.5-9B on HealthBench and ResearchQA, plus 4 out-of-domain benchmarks, 30 epochs. A hidden GPT-5.1 grader evaluates (✓ §4).
- *Key results:* up to +20.63 on HealthBench and +20.31 on ResearchQA over the base, and up to +8.06 on the six-benchmark macro average (✓ abstract and §1). HealthBench keeps improving through 45 epochs on Qwen3-4B (✓ Fig. 1b caption).
- *Limitations* (✓ §6): two model configurations; one 45-epoch run; rubric generation and judging inherit the deployed model's biases.
- *Critique.* The judge is the same model that is being trained. There is no seed variance on training.

**12. Intrinsic-confidence rewards: INTUITOR / RENT / EMPO / No Free Lunch** ([2505.19590](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.19590) ICLR'26; [2505.22660](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22660); [2504.05812](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.05812); [2506.17219](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17219))
- *What they do.* Reward = self-certainty (INTUITOR), negative entropy (RENT), or semantic-cluster entropy (EMPO).
- *Key results:*
  - INTUITOR matches GRPO on math and generalizes better to code (◐).
  - EMPO lifts Qwen2.5-Math-7B math from 30.7 to 48.1, and Qwen2.5-7B MMLU-Pro from 32.1 to 50.1 (◐).
  - No Free Lunch finds that RLIF helps early, then degrades below the pre-training model, with little gain on instruct models (◐).
- *Critiques:*
  - Spurious Rewards (✓ abstract/§1): GRPO's clipping bias amplifies high-prior behaviors (Qwen2.5-Math "code reasoning" rises from 65% to over 90%) even with random rewards. The effect is model-specific.
  - In the URLVR-scale study (✓ §4.1.2), entropy rewards give repetition collapse and probability rewards give length collapse.
  - In GMAE's head-to-head, INTUITOR and EM-RL are among the weakest label-free baselines, though CoVo is lower at 4B and 8B (✓ Table 1).

**13. Selective-Complementary RL (SCRL) / DDRL / PC-Dr.DPO** — the "fix the pseudo-label" line ([2603.19880](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.19880), [2604.21327](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.21327), [2611.09872](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.09872); CASIA (Liang group) ×2, and MBZUAI / Melbourne / Tokyo)
- *What they do:*
  - SCRL abstains from a positive label when consensus is weak, and adds entropy-gated *negative* labels (◐).
  - DDRL finds that medium-consistency prompts form an "ambiguity region" that is the main source of reward noise, and that GRPO's group normalization *amplifies* it. It applies frequency-based sampling, fixed debiased advantages, and an off-policy consensus refinement stage (◐; ✓ §2.3 heading).
  - PC-Dr.DPO splits majority-vote error into *population-majority bias*, which cannot be identified without labels, and *finite-rollout variation*, which can be mitigated. It uses prompt-conditional robust DPO plus a replay cache. It matches or beats the strongest TTRL baseline in 24/30 settings (✓ abstract and §1).
- *Limitations.* None of them can touch population-majority bias, the confidently-wrong mode. That needs an external signal (S4) or a little labeled data (TRUER).

**14. Test-time Recursive Thinking (TRT)** ([2602.03094](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.03094), Feb 2026; MSR / UCSD) — the weight-free control
- *What it does.* Per round, the model generates K rollouts under specific strategies, self-ranks them, writes "what to avoid" into a knowledge list, and proposes new strategies. No weights change.
- *Key results* (✓ Fig. 1/3):
  - LiveCodeBench-v6 hard: o4-mini 63.5 → 73.9 and o3 57.1 → 71.9 over 8 rounds, versus RSA at 70.4 / 69.7.
  - gpt-oss-120b and Qwen3-235B reach 100% on AIME-25.
  - Code runs use self-designed test execution, which contributes 7.4 points for o4-mini (✓ §5).
- *Limitations* (✓): coding needs an execution environment; there is a residual selection gap; cost grows linearly with rounds.
- *Relevance.* The comparison point any weight-updating test-time method should beat at matched compute.

### Consensus, debates & contradictions

**Consensus (multiple independent full-text confirmations):**
1. **Sharpening, not discovery.**
   - Intrinsic and consensus rewards push the policy toward its own mode (✓ 2603.08660 §3).
   - Per-problem accounting finds 0.7% learned versus 21.6% degraded (✓ 2605.19444).
   - TTSP and OPST both state that coverage of the correct answer is required (✓).
2. **Rise-then-fall with scale of training data or steps.**
   - SRT collapse (✓). URLVR-scale: ≤128 stable vs ≥512 collapse (✓). Collective-instability theory (◐). Kernel-law lock-in (◐).
   - The usual knobs (KL, GRPO vs RLOO) do not fix it; a lower learning rate delays it (✓ SRT Fig. 8).
3. **Base-model dependence.** Qwen models are more stable and LLaMA models collapse fast (✓ 2603.08660 §6.1). Spurious and random rewards work mainly on Qwen2.5-Math (✓ 2506.10947 §1). Most positive results are on Qwen.
4. **Grounding helps when the checker is good, and hurts when it is weak** (✓ T3RL §6 / App. Table 8; ◐ JURY-RL; ✓ TTSP verifier sweep).
5. **Dense self-distillation beats scalar agreement RL on the same self-generated signal** (✓ OPST Table 1: +7.3 vs +1.0 for GRPO; ◐ CANON, U-OPSD, STONE).

**Debates and contradictions:**
- **Does majority vote "add information"?**
  - Prompt-level view (He et al.): no, it only sharpens.
  - Batch-level view (Wilson et al. ✓): it transfers information across prompts. Wrong-majority prompts gain correct majorities at about 3× the resampling rate, and TTRL's average beats the initial maj@64 (✓ TTRL Fig. 7).
  - Both can hold. The batch-level equivalence is *local* (✓), and collapse appears when errors become coherent, for example through a shared template answer.
- **Is "lucky hit" reassurance or a warning?** TTRL argues weak models get *more* accurate rewards because their errors are scattered (✓ §4.2). Extinction-window, SCRL and DDRL show that medium-consistency prompts are exactly where spurious positives get amplified. Weak consensus is not harmless once group normalization rescales it.
- **Does GRPO's normalization help or hurt?**
  - DDRL: it amplifies spurious signals (◐).
  - Three Regimes: normalization leaves stability boundaries unchanged when exploration passes through it, and shifts them (by about 2–3×) when it bypasses it (✓ §1).
  - Wilson et al.: dividing by the group standard deviation moves c∞ by at most 0.010 (✓ §2).
  - The claims are at different levels (amplitude vs direction) and are not yet reconciled.
- **Small data: safe or useless?** URLVR-scale says small datasets and test-time training are the safe use (✓ §5). SRT says the gains are comparable to RLVR on full training sets before collapse (✓ Table 1). The practical recipe — stop early, use a small or transductive set, prefer Qwen — has no label-free stopping rule (OPST limitation ✓).
- **Benchmarks and contamination.** TTRL trains on AIME (30 problems) and MATH-500 test sets. TTRL alignment is now proposed as a *benchmarking* tool (◐ Gbqu33OFyN). Reported gains therefore partly measure format and familiarity, a point also made by the spurious-reward results.
- **"Label-free" is used loosely.** T3RL, JURY-RL, ASCENT and TTSP use executors, provers or environment success flags. SERPO uses a GPT-5.1 grader only for evaluation. TRUER uses labeled source data.
- **Is this recursive self-improvement?** T3RL calls TTRL a recursive self-improvement paradigm (✓ abstract). By Duan et al.'s structural-vs-effective distinction, none of these papers revises the improvement mechanism (the reward rule) and shows a better successor under matched budgets. CoVerRL's co-evolving verifier is the closest, and it is ◐ only.

### Open problems

1. **Separate learning from sharpening, by default.** Report per-problem migration (initial vs final label accuracy, as in 2605.19444) and large-k pass@k next to pass@1 and maj@k. Include a random-reward placebo arm (2506.10947, 2610.01066) and at least one non-Qwen family. Almost no method paper does all three.
2. **Error-coherence diagnostics before training.** Wilson et al. show coherence decides success. Can a cheap gradient-sketch coherence score at step 0 predict Model Collapse Step, the collective N_c, or kernel-law lock-in, and so tell you when to switch to grounded rewards?
3. **Population-majority bias.** No label-free method can correct a confidently wrong mode (PC-Dr.DPO's own decomposition). Open question: what is the minimum external signal (bits per prompt) that removes it? Candidates are TRUER-style rectifiers, cheap tools and small labeled sets.
4. **Label-free stopping and model selection.** Collapse is sudden (SRT), yet papers commonly pick peak checkpoints with gold labels, as in SRT Table 1 "peak performance". A label-free early-stopping rule (flip rate, KL spike, self-reward slope) that is validated across families is missing.
5. **Open-ended and agentic domains.**
   - SERPO's self-rubrics are judged by the trained model.
   - Score saturation and self-reward-fidelity results predict collapse.
   - Safety-in-mixed-streams shows refusal-template collapse.

   There is no study of long-horizon self-reward fidelity in agents. ASCENT side-steps it with an environment verifier.
6. **Matched-compute baselines.** Weight-updating test-time RL rarely compares with weight-free test-time scaling (TRT, functional majority voting, rejection sampling) at equal FLOPs. TTSP and ASCENT are exceptions.
7. **Heterogeneous and adversarial streams.** Online test-time RL on mixed traffic amplifies whatever the reward scores most easily (◐ mjNZLUFK21), and prompt-level attacks inflate self-reward (◐ IVFASEtqp6). No defense has been validated across methods.
8. **Effective recursion.** Can the reward-construction mechanism be revised by the system (a self-written reward rule or verifier) and shown to produce better successors under independent evaluation? Duan's "effective recursion" test is unmet in this whole corner.
9. **Weights vs harness at test time.** ASCENT beats harness methods on ALFWorld (✓). But "Where should agents adapt" (◐ 2611.19700) and harness-evolution results elsewhere in the atlas leave open when weight updates beat memory or skills, and whether gains compose.
10. **Coverage floor.** TTSP fails below mean@512 ≈ 0.1. Does any label-free method lift problems the base model has near-zero coverage on, beyond the 0.7% "learned"?

### Where it is heading (to mid-2027)

- **Consolidation into label-free self-distillation.** On-policy self-distillation toward a consensus- or stepping-stone-conditioned teacher (U-OPSD, CANON, OPST, STONE, RCTS, ASCENT) is displacing scalar majority-vote GRPO. Expect "privileged-context design" to be the main design axis, along with audits such as 2611.16064 (◐) asking whether privileged information really gives privileged guidance.
- **Hybrid grounding as the default.** Votes propose; tools, Lean, execution or small labeled rectifiers dispose. Papers that use pure intrinsic rewards will be expected to show a cross-family placebo.
- **A theory wave.** Batch coherence, collective N_c, kernel-law lock-in and three-regime exploration bounds appeared within weeks of each other (Oct–Nov 2026). Expect a unifying account and practical monitors (flip rate, Model Collapse Step) in training stacks by mid-2027.
- **Moving into agents and open-ended tasks.** Online test-time training for agents (ASCENT, HIRE kbCX1FVPSj ◐), rubric test-time RL (SERPO, RuACT, Rubric Curriculum RL ◐), and test-time RL for multimodal, video and diffusion LMs (many ICLR'27 submissions ◐).
- **ICLR 2027 decisions (late January)** will likely accept several "fix the vote" papers (GMAE, TRUER, SelectTTRL, SPINE, TCCA) and the audits (safety vulnerabilities, score saturation, SRO fragility). This will raise the evidence bar for NeurIPS 2027 submissions: per-problem accounting, placebo arms, non-Qwen bases, and label-free stopping.
- **Self-referential weight editing** ("LMs Can Rewrite Their Own Weights", ✓ §1 for scale results) may open a separate line: weight edits made by the model's own reasoning rather than by gradients. Right now it depends on graded answers and 27B scale.

### Connection to our ideas

Dan's ideas (`ONE_PAGERS.md`) work at the harness and improver level, not the weight level. This corner still supplies mechanisms, controls and threats for them:

- **#3 Gate, Not Willingness, and the N_e / bloat idea → Wilson et al. (2610.20898).**
  - A majority-vote reward is a *gate* built from noisy self-evaluations.
  - Their result — *coherence of errors, not error rate*, decides whether the gate tracks truth, and random flips average out with batch size while shared-rule errors leave a floor — maps directly onto harness gates.
  - For harness gates, the coherent error is a shared evaluator bias across validation tasks. That is the failure a "keep it if the score went up" gate cannot average away.
  - A cheap borrowed measurement for #3 is the cosine between gate decisions and oracle decisions on held-out tasks, split into coherent and incoherent parts. It is a quantitative answer to "proposer vs gate".
- **#5 Order-0 Rewards Breed Routers.** This corner is the cleanest weight-level evidence that self-consistency rewards select the cheapest pattern the reward can score:
  - template `\boxed{1}` collapse (SRT ✓);
  - refusal-template collapse (◐ mjNZLUFK21);
  - GRPO, rewarding agreement with self-generated answers, barely moves the model while dense context-conditioning does (OPST ✓).

  Cite these as the weight-level analogue of "router edits". The meta-reward comparison can borrow the placebo-twin design from Spurious Rewards, the random-reward probe and the zero-data self-play placebo trial.
- **Improvement by Inheritance / "one good early edit" → lock-in results.**
  - Extinction-window (✓), kernel-law (◐) and URLVR-scale (✓) all show that outcomes are decided *early* and are irreversible under self-reinforcement.
  - That supports reading inheritance-dominated gains as a lock-in phenomenon.
  - Flip rate and Model Collapse Step are cheap *diagnostics* to add to nested replay. They track how fast an improver lineage stops exploring.
- **#1 Taught, Not Selected.** The DDRL finding that group-relative normalization *amplifies* the noisiest signals, and PC-Dr.DPO's split into population bias vs finite-sample variation, give a vocabulary for "what the reflector reads" vs "what the score selects". Population bias corresponds to a systematically misleading transcript, which no amount of resampling fixes.
- **#6 Meta-Overfitting.** Label-free RL generalizes out of distribution in some reports (TTRL Fig. 4 †; URLVR §5.3 ✓) but regresses in others (OPST MATH-500 −4.9 ✓; TTRL GPQA −1.4 on Qwen2.5-Math-7B ✓). That is precedent that "home" sharpening can hurt far domains, which supports #6's prediction.
- **A cheap pilot, and a scoop check.**
  - A label-free *harness gate*: accept an edit if the majority of K replays agree it helps, then compare against an oracle gate. This would test the Wilson coherence criterion at the harness level.
  - Our searches (alphaXiv, ICLR'27 OpenReview) found no paper applying TTRL-style consensus rewards to *improver or harness edits*. That is not exhaustive, because S2 was rate-limited.
- **Threat to the order-1 ideas.** If weight-level self-training (ASCENT, OPST) keeps beating harness evolution on agent benchmarks (ASCENT ✓ beats GEPA, ACE and MemP on ALFWorld), reviewers will ask why improvers should edit prompts at all. Ideas #7–#9 should cite ASCENT and 2611.19700 and frame harness self-editing as complementary. The "varying goals" condition is the cleanest place to argue for harness edits over weight updates.

## Self-created tools and domain or multimodal self-evolving agents

*Marks: ✓ = checked in the full text (section/table cited), either in this fact-check pass or earlier in FULLTEXT_VERIFICATION.md; ◐ = abstract only (arXiv / alphaXiv / OpenReview); † = from memory or a secondary citation, unverified. "pp" = percentage points.*

*Full texts re-opened in this fact-check pass: SEAR, VideoResearcher, ChartEvo, MetaForge, Tool-R0, SIMIT, Agent S4 (Evolving Agent Interfaces), ReTerm, The Trinity (§4.3–4.4, App. D), the Cross-Scenario survey 2611.14256, AdaRSI (abstract and intro), Agent0 and MetaAct (abstracts and intro). Flex-RSI was verified in an earlier session (FULLTEXT_VERIFICATION.md). The texts are under /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-nlp-lab-paper-search/b6ee0fee-4f54-593f-a9fa-6ec1fa49d4e7/scratchpad/papers/<id>/paper.txt.*

### At a glance
- **What this corner is.** Self-improving agents that improve their action and perception surface, not only their prompts. That surface means tools, toolchains, interfaces and code policies. The corner also covers domain loops (multimodal, video, chart, GUI/OS, terminal, embodied), where self-improvement has to cope with expensive rollouts and weak verifiers.
- **Duan 2609.11873 levels.** Almost everything here is L1–L2. A human fixes the objective and the acceptance rule, and the agent chooses *what tool to build* †.
- **Dai et al. components.** In their Prompt/Memory/Skill/Harness terms, these are Skill/Harness updates with "persistent experience" (pattern ii). They are almost never "improver update" (pattern iii) †.
- **Two families.**
  - (a) **Weight-space self-play over tool use**: Tool-R0, Agent0, AgentForge, Marvo, RarePlay, and the VLM self-play line.
  - (b) **Training-free libraries of executable tools or harnesses**, built by a proposer that is usually stronger than the agent: VideoResearcher, ChartEvo, Agent S4, SEAR code-as-policy, The Trinity, AgentFactory.
  - MetaForge is the clearest hybrid. It forges tools inside GRPO and registers them into a persistent pool.
- **State of the art (each is a single-paper claim).**
  - Long video: VideoResearcher, +2.4 average over its own base (72.1→74.5) ✓ Table 1.
  - Long-tail charts: ChartEvo, 48.0→93.6 on 9 ChartBench types ✓ Table 1.
  - Computer use: Agent S4, 21.3% binary on OSWorld-V2 with Qwen3.8-27B ✓ Table 2.
  - Multimodal tool use: MetaForge, Qwen3-VL-8B 73.8→88.1 across 12 benchmarks, averaged over 3 runs ✓ Table 1, l.447.
  - Terminal: ReTerm-9B, 34.8% on TB2.0 ✓ Table 1.
  - Robotics: SEAR is a controlled benchmark (330 simulated + 5 real tasks) with matched controls for resampling, luck, privileged state and budget ✓ §1. SEAR does not call itself the "first"; that is our judgment from the corpus †.
- **Emerging consensus.**
  - In domains bound by perception and measurement, executable tools beat instruction or skill edits. ChartEvo: evolved tools 84.4 vs skill-only 55.6 ✓ Table 4. VideoResearcher: SkillOpt scores −2.3 against the base ✓ Table 1.
  - Gains concentrate where a cheap execution check or answer key exists.
  - Libraries help most when the base model succeeds "sometimes but not reliably" (SEAR: +12.0 pts at 30–80% base success ✓ §3.2).
- **Matched-baseline gains are small.** Against a matched self-improvement baseline or the human seed, gains shrink to 1–3 points:
  - VideoResearcher vs Meta-Harness: +1.0 average (74.5 vs 73.5) ✓ Table 1.
  - Agent S4 evolved vs seed repository: +1.86 pp, about 2 of 108 tasks ✓ Table 2/4.
  - The big headline numbers compare against a weak base, use a stronger proposer model, or use oracle routing.
- **Self-built verifiers are the main hazard.**
  - SEAR: one success detector the agent built was wrong on 91% of 699 rollouts and was saved to memory as a "fact". That run scored 4.6%, against 15.5% and 23.6% for its siblings ✓ §3.3.
  - Multimodal consensus labels degrade. 24% of majority-vote labels are wrong (VQS ◐). VisPlay's pseudo-label accuracy fell 72.0→61.0 over 3 iterations (✓ via 2611.14256 §4.2).
- **Biggest open problem.** Almost nobody measures whether created tools *retain* value and *transfer* under matched budgets and several seeds.
  - The 2611.14256 survey states "No method measures retention on earlier-round goals" for multimodal reasoning (§4.4) and for GUI/Web (§6.4) ✓.
  - The same survey names one exception in generation: RSI in UMMs, where earlier-vocabulary accuracy fell 72%→60% after a round replaced that vocabulary ✓ §5.4.
  - The survey's cross-scenario portability verdicts are explicitly untested ✓ abstract.
  - The improver that writes the tools is never itself edited.

### Taxonomy
The main axis is **what persistent artifact the agent creates**. Two secondary axes are **who writes it** (the same model, a stronger proposer, or a teacher) and **what admits it** (an execution check, dev-set accuracy, a judge, or nothing).

| Approach | Persistent artifact | Writer / gate | Representative papers |
|---|---|---|---|
| A. Zero-data tool-use self-play (weights) | Policy weights; self-generated tool menus, tasks and gold calls | Same model in two roles; band-pass difficulty reward; JSON/AST match | Tool-R0 ✓, Agent0 ✓, AgentForge (O2jE6PfSFS) ◐, RarePlay (FH5OoGxsBx) ◐, Marvo 2610.15084 ◐, Self-Evolve w/ Reference 2610.09856 ◐ |
| B. Tool forging inside RL | Weights + a persistent pool of forged tools | Own policy; execution + judge gate; capacity/usage retention | MetaForge ✓, AgentForge ◐ |
| C. Training-free libraries of tools or toolchains | Python tools, macro-tools, SOP-tools, local toolchains | Usually a stronger proposer (Codex / GPT-5.6-Sol); dev-accuracy gate | VideoResearcher ✓, ChartEvo ✓, AgentFactory ◐, EvoSOP ◐, SkillSmith ◐, CoEvoSkills ◐, SkillCompiler 2610.39508 ◐, Tool-making low-latency 2607.08010 ◐, SciToolAgent-Evo 2607.28692 ◐, KG-as-Files 2610.18616 ◐ (within one episode) |
| D. Evolution of the interface / action space | Observation and action APIs plus usage knowledge; executable guards | Same model as meta-agent (S4); population selected on validation | Agent S4 ✓, MetaAct (rxyGomjMBA / 2611.20655) ✓(abstract+intro), LOTS ◐, Hybrid Computer Use 2610.41432 ◐ (human-designed) |
| E. Self-generated multimodal supervision | Synthetic (Q, A, image/video) items or programs; weights or ICL demos | Same model; renderer, program or self-verifier | SIMIT ✓, VQS (3ijW6lQHLT) ◐, Tempo-Zero (cizDyhcm7v) ◐, VisPlay † (via survey ✓), Trinity-VLM 2610.04469 ◐, RISE ◐, UniEvo-VL 2609.38721 ◐ |
| F. Embodied code-as-policy and skill libraries | Control code, skills, lessons; sometimes VLA fine-tunes | Frontier LM; success predicate or sealed judge | SEAR ✓, AdaRSI ✓(intro), EmbodiedEvo 2610.18867 ◐, EvoRAM ◐, SERA 2610.29560 ◐, EMHO 2610.08432 ◐, ESI 2611.18176 ◐, ReSight 2610.33487 ◐, DexAgent ◐ |
| G. Training on own failures / recovery | Weights trained from the model's own failure states | Teacher SFT + GRPO with verifier reward | ReTerm ✓ |

| I. Synthesis, benchmarks, safety | — | — | 2611.14256 ✓, Flex-RSI ✓FV, EmbodiedCLBench 2610.13021 ◐, EvolvAttack ◐, EVOLVE guardrails 2611.02516 ◐ |

### Paper cards

**SEAR: Self-Evolving Agentic Robotics** ([2610.18792](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18792), v1 13 Oct 2026, Luma AI ✓ header)
- *What it does.* Runs frontier LMs as self-evolving robot agents in three modes: code-as-policy, agent-as-policy, and auto-research that fine-tunes a VLA. Matched controls separate learning from resampling, familiarity, privileged state, budget and luck ✓ §1–2.
- *Setup.*
  - 7 LMs; 330 simulated tasks in 5 families and 2 physics engines; 5 physical tasks on a two-arm rig.
  - More than four years of agent runtime in total; 1 h per simulated task and 12 h per real task ✓ Fig. 1, §4.4.
  - Controls: best-of-3 at equal total budget, runs with no library ("Vanilla"), and a sealed judge that grades the frozen policy ✓ §2. Simulated results use three runs per condition ✓ §3.2.
- *Key results.*
  - The library's gain depends on base skill. Mean +12.0 pts when no-library TEST success is 30–80% (15 pairs), +3.0 below 30%, +0.9 above 80%. A quadratic fit over 25 pairs peaks at a 43% base (+14.7) ✓ §3.2 Fig.
  - GPT-5.6-sol on RoboLab: 46.9% with no library, 42.4% with its **own** library, 60.6% with the library Opus wrote, 55.7% with Kimi-k3's ✓ §3.2.
  - An agent-built verifier declared success on 699 later rollouts and was wrong on 91% of them. Because it was also the stopping rule, 637 rollouts ended early, and it was kept in memory. The run scored 4.6%, against 15.5% and 23.6% for its siblings ✓ §3.3.
  - Run-to-run spread: two DeepSeek-v4-flash Lineage runs differ by 20.9 pts ✓ §3.3.
  - Generalisation tiers for Opus code policies: 94.4 (LIBERO TEST) → 66.0 (LIBERO-RIG hardware faults) → 47.7 (scene changes) ✓ §4.1.
  - Real robot, code-as-policy (CaP): Fable 5.1 70.2, GPT-6-astra 41.4, Opus 5 35.6. Acting live (agent-as-policy, AaP) lifts GPT-6-astra to 88.0 ✓ §4.4, Table 4.
  - Six practice runs reached ten successes in a row. Only one of them (Fable's Push-T) then succeeded on all ten staged scenes, and two succeeded on only four ✓ §4.4.
- *Limitations / critiques.*
  - Each real-robot entry is one practice run ✓ Table 4 caption.
  - Only skills and memories persist between tasks; the harness and the improver are fixed ✓ §2, l.239 and discussion l.3415.
  - Within the time budget, practice with self-reset under-samples hard starts. Only 10 of Opus's 64 Push-T starts needed a turn of more than 90°, against 6 of the 10 staged scenes ✓ §4.4.
  - The survey 2611.14256 cites SEAR as its example of erroneous writes spreading across later rollouts ✓ §3.6.

**VideoResearcher: Self-Improving Tool Design for Long-Video Understanding** ([2609.19664](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19664), v1 17 Sep 2026, JHU, preprint ✓ header)
- *What it does.* A training-free, multi-agent Evolving loop: Auditor → Analyzer → Designer → Coder → Debugger → fixed Evaluator → Verifier → Memory. It writes Python video tools on top of a single `ask_video` primitive. The Worker and the perception model stay fixed.
- *Setup.*
  - Worker GPT-5.6-SOL; perception model Qwen3.5-4B (served on 8×B200); Evolving roles run on the Codex SDK.
  - 300 ALLVB dev questions (videos average nearly two hours); up to 20 rounds.
  - A tool is accepted only if it *strictly* improves dev accuracy. Tests use LVBench, LongVideoBench and Video-MME, kept out of tool design and selection ✓ §4.1.
- *Key results.*
  - Average 72.1→74.5 ✓ Table 1.
  - Baselines on the same base: SkillOpt 69.8 (−2.3), Meta-Harness 73.5 (+1.4), AutoResearch 71.7 (−0.4) ✓ Table 1.
  - Table 3 lists five representative rounds. Two tools were accepted: Scene Landmark Index in Round 2 (dev 68.7→75.0) and Window Atomic Scan in Round 7 (75.0→76.7). Rounds 3, 14 and 17 were rejected ✓ Table 3, §4.4.
  - The final test scores equal the Round-7 scores, so no later round was accepted. The paper does not report how many rounds ran in total or the full rejection count.
  - Round 7 is *below* Round 2 on LVBench (68.4 vs 68.9) and LongVideoBench (75.0 vs 75.5); it is above on Video-MME (80.2 vs 80.0) ✓ Table 2b.
- *Limitations / critiques.*
  - The authors concede that the framework relies on textual trajectory assessment and "repeated selection on one development set" ✓ §5.
  - Selection on the dev set added +8.0 dev points (68.7→76.7) but only +1.0 to +4.1 on test columns (+2.4 average). With 300 questions the dev standard error is about 2.5 pp (my calculation), so a strict-increase gate admits noise.
  - No repeated runs are reported.
  - The Verifier's "Causal Verification Report" is "not an independent causal experiment" ✓ §3.3.

**ChartEvo: Self-Evolving Agent Harnesses for Long-Tail Chart Reasoning** ([2610.28282](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28282), v1 20 Oct 2026, CASIA/UCAS, preprint ✓ header)
- *What it does.* Evolves three things together for chart types where MLLMs fail: Skills, executable Tools, and "Self-Evolving Local Toolchains" (SELT, frozen tool compositions).
- *Setup.*
  - Agent Qwen3.7-Plus; **proposer GPT-5.6-Sol** ✓ §4.1.
  - 100 training questions per chart type, with ground truth used for evolution. 9 ChartBench types (450 test Q) and 8 ChartX types (265 test Q) ✓ §4, App.
  - 5% relative-error tolerance; action budget of 15 ✓ §4.
- *Key results.*
  - ChartBench 48.0→93.6. The abstract's "45.6%" means percentage points. GPT-5.6-Sol answering directly scores 68.9 ✓ Table 1.
  - ChartX 53.6→86.1, against GPT-5.6-Sol at 84.4 ✓ Table 2.
  - Ablation on 5 ChartBench types: base 42.8, skill-only 55.6, base harness 57.2, evolved tools 84.4, full 94.8 ✓ Table 4.
  - SELT cuts API calls from 6.19 to 2.73 while accuracy goes from 91.2 to 94.8 ✓ Table 6.
  - Cost per question: 2,907 tokens and 68.8 s, against 2,454.5 tokens and 42.7 s for the base ✓ Table 3.
- *Limitations / critiques.*
  - This is distillation from a stronger proposer, not self-improvement of the agent model.
  - About 30–50 test Q per chart type; a single run; evolution and test data come from the same distribution.
  - The authors flag overly specialised harness components and distribution shift between evolution and test data ✓ Limitations.

**MetaForge: A Self-Evolving Multimodal Agent that Retrieves, Adapts, and Forges Tools On Demand** ([2606.01801](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.01801), v1 1 Jun 2026, ECNU/ZJU et al., preprint ✓ header)
- *What it does.* Splits behaviour into four steps: Decide, Retrieve, Adapt, Forge.
  - A forged tool (Markdown spec + schema + Python) enters the pool only if it executes *and* a judge model says it matches its description.
  - Training is multi-turn GRPO with a composite reward, and forging is rewarded only in correct trajectories.
  - The pool has a capacity limit, semantic dedup, and retention by usage (threshold Q3 + 1.5·IQR) ✓ §3.4.
- *Setup.* Qwen3-VL-8B on VerlTool, 8×H200. 12 image-text benchmarks with IID/OOD splits for both datasets and tools; 16 baselines. "All reported results are averaged over three independent runs" ✓ §4, l.447.
- *Key results.*
  - Average over all benchmarks: 73.80→88.14 (IID tools) and 74.21→88.98 (OOD tools), against Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 86.88 ✓ Table 1.
  - Forging: 190 attempts / 123 registered (IID); 12 / 11 (OOD) ✓ Table 2.
- *Limitations / critiques.*
  - Image-text only; no audio, video, temporal or interactive settings ✓ Limitations.
  - The semantic gate is an LLM judge.
  - GRPO is keyed to answers, so this is supervised RL, not zero-data.
  - Some closed-model baselines look anomalous, e.g. GPT-5.4 at 36.40 on CLEVR-M ✓ Table 1.

**Tool-R0: Self-Evolving LLM Agents for Tool-Learning from Zero Data** ([2602.21320](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.21320), v1 24 Feb 2026, UIUC/ETH, preprint ✓ header; "83 votes" †)
- *What it does.* A Generator trained with GRPO writes (question, tool menu, gold call) triples near the Solver's frontier. Its reward is band-pass on the Solver's pass rate over [0.25, 0.75], with Gaussian falloff (σ = 0.12). The Solver then trains on a filtered curriculum ordered from easy to hard ✓ §3, §4.
- *Setup.*
  - Qwen2.5 0.5B/1.5B/3B and Llama-3.2-3B; 3 iterations × 50 steps; 10,000 candidates filtered to 2,000 per iteration; 3 GPUs ✓ §4, App.
  - Evaluated on 5 benchmarks (ToolAlpaca, SealTool, NexusRaven, API-Bank, SNIPS) ✓ Table 1.
- *Key results.*
  - Qwen2.5-1.5B average 24.85→47.84 (+22.99, +92.52% relative) ✓ Table 1.
  - Beats SFT on xLAM (60k), Hammer (210k), ToolACE (12k) and ToolRL (4k; 46.06) ✓ Table 2.
  - Ablations: shared weights 30.42 (−17.42), frozen Generator 41.65, no difficulty reward 43.54 ✓ Table 3.
  - Small models saturate around iteration 3 ✓ RQ8.
- *Limitations / critiques.*
  - No real tool execution. Rewards are JSON/AST matches against the Generator's own gold calls, and pseudo-labels are filtered by agreement with the Solver itself.
  - No multi-run standard errors, which the authors admit ✓ §5.2.
  - Table inconsistency: the API-Bank base score for 1.5B is 19.13 in Table 1 but 10.13 in Table 2 ✓. Table 1's average of 24.85 implies 19.13 is correct.
  - The "separate weights are essential" claim conflicts with single-policy designs such as Tempo-Zero ◐.

**SIMIT: Self-Improving VLMs via Imagination at Test-Time** ([2611.00053](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.00053), v1 stamped 11 Oct 2026, DTU/Pioneer Centre/Copenhagen ✓ header; ICLR27 sub m4ccvE2AMl)
- *What it does.* Before answering an unlabeled query, a unified model (BAGEL-7B) imagines similar problems.
  - It fixes the answer *before* generating the image, then verifies, repairs and filters by difficulty.
  - The resulting data serves as ICL demos or for fine-tuning.
  - Structured images go through a library of 17 renderers. The library is **human-written and fixed**: "We did not optimize them against benchmark scores" ✓ App. (Skill Library).
- *Setup.*
  - 17 LMMs-Eval-Lite benchmarks; 50 validation / 500 evaluation examples each ✓ App.
  - Baselines (TTRL, EMPO, TTRV, SRLM, Self-Consistency, Self-Refine) are tuned on the same validation data ✓ §4, App.
- *Key results.*
  - SIMIT-ICL: +6.98% mean relative gain at 25× runtime. Test-set FT→ICL: +7.20% at 55×. Best label-free RL baseline (TTRV): +2.07% at 41× ✓ Table 1.
  - Under TTRL on VizWiz, "unanswerable" is the majority vote in 99.2% of training steps. 79.3% of the steps with nonzero advantage still reinforce it ✓ §4.1.
  - SIMIT corrects 14.4% of initially wrong answers and disrupts 2.0% of initially correct ones. Its supervision-error rate is 12%, against 33–38% for the baselines ✓ §4.4.
  - Transfer across benchmarks: +4.3% within a domain, only +0.5% across domains ✓ §4.1.
- *Limitations / critiques.*
  - The gains are relative means over mixed metrics, CIDEr included.
  - Data quality is audited by Claude Sonnet 5, an external evaluator ✓ §4.
  - The model does not create its own tools.
  - Gains on other backbones are small: +2.21% (SenseNova-U1) and +3.97% (Lance) ✓ §4.1.

**Evolving Agent Interfaces (Agent S4)** ([2610.28601](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28601), v1 20 Oct 2026, Simular/UCSB †affiliations, tech report)
- *What it does.* A meta-agent reads unlabeled trajectories from synthetic tasks. It mutates *repositories* of interfaces plus usage knowledge, or crosses two of them over. The population is selected on validation tasks that the meta-agent never sees ✓ abstract, §3.
- *Setup.*
  - The task agent **and** the meta-agent are both Qwen3.8-27B ✓ l.394.
  - The seed repository is human-written; Table 5 lists its files and interfaces ✓ App. A.2. The earlier "about 550 lines" figure is not in the text and has been removed.
  - 30 synthetic training tasks for OSWorld V2, written by a GPT-6 Astra coordinator and GPT-5.6-Sol authors; 15 official validation tasks; 30 descendants per run ✓ Table 1, §4.
- *Key results.*
  - OSWorld-V2 binary score: no repository 15.74, seed 19.44, evolved 21.30 ✓ Table 4. Opus 4.8 scores 20.6, at $72.40 vs $1.10 per task ✓ Table 2.
  - The "3.8×" headline is measured against a different harness, Qwen CUA at 5.56 ✓ Table 2.
  - ScienceBoard 55.03→58.58 (93→99 of 169 tasks) against the seed ✓ Table 3. The abstract's 41.4→58.6 uses a different baseline.
- *Limitations / critiques.*
  - Evolution adds about 2 tasks over the seed.
  - The 15 validation tasks are included in the reported full set ✓ l.390.
  - One evolution run per strategy. Denoising was applied only on ScienceBoard, not OSWorld ✓ §4.
  - The variant evolved with a scratch VM gets a higher partial score (51.06 vs 46.90) but its binary score (19.44) only equals the seed ✓ Table 2/4.

**ReTerm: Recovery Training for Self-Improving Terminal Agents** ([2610.18484](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18484), v2 14 Oct 2026, Fudan/CUHK/SJTU, preprint ✓ header)
- *What it does.*
  - Snapshots the VM at the base model's failure states.
  - A teacher (DeepSeek-V4-Pro) writes recoveries from those states. After filtering this gives ReTerm-10K, used for SFT.
  - ReTerm-GRPO then forks recovery rollouts from the evolving policy's own failure states, kept in a recency queue ✓ §3.
- *Setup.*
  - Qwen3.5-9B on 16×A100; 6K trajectories for SFT and 4K tasks for RL.
  - Each update uses 8 original and 2 recovery groups of 16 rollouts.
  - Inference at temperature 1.0 "with the task seed fixed at 0" ✓ §4.1.
- *Key results.*
  - TB2.0 20.2→34.8; TBLite 44.2→60.6; SWE-bench Verified 45.2→58.4 ✓ Table 1.
  - Ablation: SFT 25.8, GRPO 28.0, ReTerm-GRPO 34.8 ✓ Table 4.
  - Transfer to three other harnesses: +6.7 to +12.4 ✓ Table 2.
  - AIME25 73.3→93.3 ✓ Table 3.
  - Recovery rates stay at or below 32% for every error type except tool-use errors ✓ §4.5.
- *Limitations / critiques.*
  - "Self-improving" applies only to the RL phase; the cold start is distillation from a teacher.
  - A single sample on small benchmarks (TB2.0 has about 89 tasks †). The +6.8 over GRPO is about 6 tasks.
  - The AIME25 jump is 6 of 30 problems.

**The Trinity: Capability-Driven RSI for Multimodal Agents** ([2610.36077](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.36077), v2 30 Oct 2026, "The Trinity Research Team" ✓ header)
- *What it does.* Three roles, Creator, Explorer and Evolver, build a capability tree over heterogeneous benchmarks. They generate simplified, verifiable simulated worlds per capability ("Real2Sim2Real") and evolve a harness tree, which a capability-aware router selects from ✓ abstract, §3.
- *Setup.* Frozen Claude Opus 5 on a Prime Agent base harness; 28 Train / 18 Unseen benchmarks, including 2 real-world embodied tasks ✓ §4, Table 1. Some environments are "agent-built from web-searched sources" ✓ Table 1.
- *Key results.*
  - Over 4 iterations, Train 39.1→73.2 and Unseen 42.1→64.1. Reference harnesses: Codex 47.5, DeepSeek 46.2 ✓ §4.3.
  - Eleusis declines 82.2→81.1 between iterations 1 and 4 ✓ §4.3.
  - With the router choosing for itself, the scores are 71.27 Train / 60.96 Unseen, against Oracle 73.16 / 63.61 ✓ §4.4 Table 4.
- *Limitations / critiques.*
  - Evaluation uses "the best-scoring compatible node Harness under the Oracle setting", plus skills from five preparation trials per benchmark–harness pair ✓ §4, App. D. This inflates "Unseen".
  - No repeated seeds; benchmark environments are partly rebuilt by agent web search.

**A Cross-Scenario Survey and Analysis of Self-Evolving Multimodal Agents** ([2611.14256](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.14256), v1 10 Nov 2026, Jingjing Jiang ✓ header; also on the ICLR27 list)
- *What it does.*
  - Defines a self-evolving multimodal agent by four criteria plus a differentia of self-reference ✓ §1–2.
  - Places four scenarios (multimodal reasoning, generation, GUI/Web, embodied manipulation) on ceilings of rollout count × feedback fidelity.
  - Judges each mechanism portable / conditional / blocked / redundant across scenarios ✓ abstract.
- *Key results.*
  - Five cross-cycle degradation modes: compounding reward hacking, distribution shift, forgetting/plasticity loss, curriculum collapse, model collapse ✓ §3.6, Table 6.
  - "No method measures retention on earlier-round goals" is stated for multimodal reasoning (§4.4) and GUI/Web (§6.4) ✓.
  - For generation, the survey states "Only RSI in UMMs measures retention on earlier-round goals" (72%→60%) ✓ §5.4.
  - In reasoning, a guard on retention exists only where gated training-free writes keep a fixed reference ✓ §4.3–4.4.
  - Pseudo-label accuracy falls: VisPlay 72.0→61.0 over three iterations, Video-Zero 64.5→37.5 over five ✓ §4.2.
- *Limitations.* The verdicts are inferred from evidence within single scenarios and are "still untested". The survey proposes measurements that could overturn them ✓ abstract.

**AdaRSI: On-Demand RSI for Embodied Agents** ([2610.20474](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20474), v2 17 Nov 2026, NEU/AgiBot ✓ header)
- *What it does.* A coding agent first fixes harness tools and procedures. Only sub-steps that remain unreliable get demos the agent collects itself. These are validated by temporary fine-tuning probes and pooled into a specialist VLA that works alongside the original executor ✓ abstract.
- *Key results.*
  - RoboCasa365 unseen composite tasks: 4.6→13.3, against 9.9 for the harness alone ✓ abstract/intro.
  - Perturbed LIBERO-Pro 2.0 tasks: 32.9→49.1, against 39.1 for the harness alone ✓ intro.
  - Beats adapting every manipulation sub-step (13.3 vs 11.1) while using 34% of the GPU time and 36% of the demos ✓ intro.
- *Limitations.* Read only as far as the intro. Absolute success on composite tasks is low.

**Flex-RSI** ([2611.08946](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.08946), v1 6 Nov 2026, TAMU + 12 institutions †affiliations)
- *What it does.* 24 vision/robotics tasks × 18 models. The executor edits the solution behind a 2σ held-out gate. The improver edits the harness, including itself, under a 400-line cap. A frozen-improver arm is included ✓FV.
- *Key results.*
  - The improver adds 0.0 in the single frontier pair, which is at ceiling (a replicate scored 40).
  - For open models it adds +2 to +40, and only 3 of 6 deltas fall in +20 to +40.
  - Every pair is n=1, and one episode is worth 20 points ✓ (FULLTEXT_VERIFICATION).
- *Relevance.* The only multimodal or robotics benchmark with a frozen-improver control that we found (corpus claim †).

### Consensus, debates & contradictions
- **Tools beat instructions in domains bound by perception.**
  - ChartEvo: tools 84.4 vs skills 55.6 ✓ Table 4.
  - VideoResearcher: SkillOpt −2.3; the Meta-Harness and AutoResearch runs "mainly revise prompts, yielding limited gains" ✓ §4.2.
  - Agent S4 points the same way through interfaces.
  - This *contradicts* text-domain findings that the effective edit surface collapses to instruction text (IbI, round 3). The likely reason is that a perception bottleneck needs new observations, not new advice. The best edit surface depends on the domain.
- **"Self"-improvement here is mostly improvement by a stronger model.**
  - ChartEvo (GPT-5.6-Sol proposer), VideoResearcher (Codex evolvers), ReTerm (DeepSeek-V4-Pro teacher) and EmbodiedEvo (experience from a stronger model) are all at least partly distillation.
  - True same-model loops show much smaller deltas. Agent S4, with Qwen3.8-27B as its own meta-agent, gains +1.86 pp over the seed ✓. SIMIT reaches about +7% relative only with heavy compute (25–55×) ✓.
  - Flex-RSI fits a "teacher gap" reading: 0.0 in its one frontier pair, which sits at ceiling, against +2 to +40 for open models, all n=1 ✓FV.
- **Libraries are not monotone.**
  - Gated systems never report regressions, because by construction they keep only gains (VideoResearcher, ChartEvo).
  - SEAR inherits without a gate and finds a model's own library *hurting* it (46.9→42.4) while other models' libraries help ✓.
  - VideoResearcher's later round scores below its earlier round on 2 of 3 test sets ✓. Gating hides drift; it does not prevent overfitting to the dev set.
- **Role separation is unresolved.** Tool-R0 finds that sharing Generator/Solver weights costs −17.42 ✓. Tempo-Zero and Agent0-VL-style designs use one policy for both roles ◐. The answer may depend on how high-entropy the action space is.
- **Verifier provenance decides everything.**
  - Consensus or self-judged labels degrade: VisPlay 72→61 ✓ via survey; TTRL makes "unanswerable" the majority vote in 99.2% of VizWiz steps ✓ SIMIT.
  - Answers grounded in a program or a render (SIMIT, VQS, Tempo-Zero) correct more errors.
  - Agent-built verifiers can be catastrophic: SEAR's detector was wrong on 91% of the rollouts where it declared success ✓.
- **Evidence quality is weak.**
  - Single runs and tiny test sets dominate. ChartEvo has about 30–50 Q per type; ReTerm samples once with the task seed fixed at 0; VideoResearcher reports no repetitions.
  - Only MetaForge (3 runs) and SEAR (3 runs in simulation) report repetition among the papers here.
  - SEAR shows that run-to-run spreads of 20.9 pts exist ✓. Most claimed deltas in this corner are within plausible run noise.

### Open problems
1. **Retention of created tools.** Almost no paper re-tests earlier-round goals after later tools are added. The survey finds none in reasoning or GUI/Web, and one in generation, RSI in UMMs (2611.14256 §4.4, §5.4, §6.4 ✓). We need a survival curve per tool and per round on frozen earlier tasks.
2. **Matched-budget controls outside robotics.** SEAR's design (best-of-3, no-library, sealed judge) ✓ has not been ported to tool creation for video, charts, GUI or terminals. Every headline there lacks a "resample K times" arm.
3. **Teacher vs self.** No paper crosses proposer strength with agent strength, for example a ChartEvo grid of proposer ∈ {self, stronger} × agent. Without that grid, "self-improvement" and "distillation" cannot be told apart.
4. **Noise in dev-set gates.** A strict-increase gate on 300 Q (VideoResearcher) or 15 validation tasks (Agent S4) admits noise. Tool-creation loops need sequential or statistical gates, which already exist for text harnesses.
5. **Who writes the verifier.** When the agent builds its own success detector or semantic judge (SEAR, MetaForge's judge, CoEvoSkills' surrogate), how often is it wrong, and does inheritance compound the error? SEAR gives one anecdote, not a rate.
6. **The improver is frozen everywhere.** The tool-*making* procedure is never edited: not VideoResearcher's Evolving loop, ChartEvo's proposer, S4's meta-agent (fixed model and harness ✓ §3) or Trinity's Evolver. Pattern-(iii) updates are absent from this whole corner.
7. **Tool drift and deprecation.** Created tools break when upstream APIs, apps or perception models change. Only the industrial report (2607.08010 ◐) and Δτ-Bench † touch this. Nobody studies how to maintain a tool library under real version changes.
8. **Portability is untested.** The survey's portable/conditional/blocked/redundant verdicts ✓ are predictions. For example, program-verified QA should port to GUI only where outcomes can be checked. One matched-budget study of cross-scenario transfer would confirm or falsify several verdicts at once.
9. **Security of persistent tools and memories.** EvolvAttack (dormant until memory evolves ◐) and inherited wrong verifiers show that audits of a clean initial state miss threats that grow later.

### Where it is heading (to mid-2027)
- **The measurement turn reaches multimodal and embodied work.** Expect SEAR-style controls (best-of-k, no-library, sealed judge, 3+ runs) to become a reviewer expectation for tool-creation papers, as frozen-improver arms did for text harnesses (Flex-RSI, SelfImprove-Bench †). Expect several audits finding that "matched-budget tool evolution adds ≤2 pp".
- **Program-grounded self-supervision replaces consensus** in VLM self-play: VQS ◐, Tempo-Zero ◐, SIMIT ✓. Expect render and program verifiers to become standard, and majority-vote baselines to be treated as straw men.
- **RL with forging.** RL-trained tool forging (MetaForge, AgentForge) will likely merge with zero-data curricula (Tool-R0). The weights learn *when* to forge, and a gated library stores *what* was forged.
- **Interfaces become the unit of evolution** for computer use (Agent S4), along with cheaper meta-agents that use the same model. Gains will be reported against strong human seeds, not weak harnesses.
- **Embodied systems split into two passes**: harness work first, then targeted weight adaptation (AdaRSI, ESI, EvoRAM). Real-robot evaluation will stay at about one run per cell because of cost.
- **Not expected by mid-2027** (my estimate): a tool-creation system that edits its own tool-making procedure with a measured benefit of order 1.

### Connection to our ideas
- **#1 Taught, Not Selected.** SEAR's self-built verifier is a clean field example of the *reading/writing* channel corrupting a lineage. A wrong "fact" was written to memory and inherited, not selected by the score ✓.
  - Tool creation adds a third channel next to traces and scores: *the agent's own instruments*.
  - Use SEAR §3.3 as motivation. A cheap extension: seed a buggy perception tool and measure whether evolved tools inherit the bug.
- **#2 / #3 Forced-Quota / Gate, Not Willingness (merged).** This corner gives strong outside support for the scarcity of self-edits.
  - Every system here holds its tool-*maker* fixed: VideoResearcher's Evolving agents, ChartEvo's proposer, S4's meta-agent, Trinity's Evolver.
  - VideoResearcher's strict-increase gate is a ready-made "proposed vs propagated vs paid off" funnel in a non-text domain. Its Table 3 shows 2 of 5 representative proposals accepted, and the final toolbox has 2 evolved tools ✓. The full count of rounds and rejections is not reported, so the funnel needs those numbers from the authors or a rerun.
- **#6 Meta-Overfitting.** Several findings are direct evidence and a possible testbed:
  - SEAR's cross-model library result: on GPT-5.6-sol, its own library −4.5 and Opus's library +13.7 ✓.
  - VideoResearcher's degradation from selection on the dev set ✓.
  - ChartEvo's evolution per benchmark ✓.
  - SEAR's "control code and shared routines transfer, while task-specific solutions do not" ✓ is the procedure-vs-memory split the idea predicts.
- **#7 Varying Goals.** Tool libraries are the natural object for DriftStream: versioned tools under real library changes. The industrial report's "versioned tools expose upstream data drift" ◐ is anecdotal support. No paper here varies the switching rate.
- **#8 Openness Ladder.** This chapter bears on #8 most strongly.
  - Domains bound by perception reward opening the *tool* surface. ChartEvo: tools ≫ skills ✓.
  - In VideoResearcher, tool-level evolution (74.5) beats harness-level Meta-Harness (73.5), whole-system AutoResearch (71.7) and prompt-level SkillOpt (69.8) ✓ Table 1. Whole-system search beats prompt-only here, so the ordering is not "prompt > whole-system". The paper says whole-system search "may largely waste effort on unrelated components" ✓ §1.
  - Text domains favour instruction-only surfaces (IbI).
  - Together these fit "the optimum is in the middle and *moves*". A two-domain openness sweep (text vs chart/video) with matched budgets would be novel and cheap to build on ChartEvo's released setting. The risk of being scooped is moderate: EvoSpace (MQoRwlss2y) states the dilemma for text.
- **#9 MetaShift.** No paper here changes the *rules of improving* mid-run (e.g., swapping the acceptance gate or the perception model). VideoResearcher assumes fixed perception ✓, which makes a mid-run swap of the perception model a natural MetaShift probe.
- **#4 / #5 (Order-2 audit, routers).** Weak links. The Trinity's capability router and oracle node selection ✓ are an example of an order-0 reward producing a *router*. Note that its self-routing gives 71.27/60.96 against Oracle's 73.16/63.61 ✓ Table 4. This supports #5's framing if cited carefully.

## Deployment-grounded RSI with human feedback and oversight (production, personal and team agents)

*Scope.* This chapter covers self-improvement loops whose experience, feedback or acceptance decision comes from real deployment: users, operators, reviewers and production traffic. It does not cover loops fed only by benchmarks or self-generated tasks. It also covers the human-oversight machinery that decides which self-generated changes go live.

*Reading.* I read 15 papers in full or near-full; their text is cached under `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-nlp-lab-paper-search/b6ee0fee-4f54-593f-a9fa-6ec1fa49d4e7/scratchpad/papers/<id>/`. The other roughly 40 papers come from abstracts: alphaXiv, ICLR 2027 OpenReview, and Semantic Scholar forward citations. A fact-check pass (2026-11-19) re-opened 16 cached full texts; corrections are listed in the log at the end.

*Marks.* ✓ means checked in full text this session. ◐ means abstract only. † means from project notes or memory and not re-checked.

*ID note.* Three identifiers in this chapter are alphaXiv slugs, not arXiv ids: `2611.rri`, `2611.always-on-personal-intelligence` and `2611.recursive-self-improvement-llm-agents`. They do not resolve on arxiv.org and need their real arXiv ids before citation †.

### At a glance

- **What this corner is.** These loops close on human or production signals rather than benchmark scores. There are four kinds:
  - **Arena votes:** RSI Arena.
  - **Production failure mining:** CARE, G-CAST, LinkedIn.
  - **Per-user corrections:** Reglos, LiveAsset, OpenClaw-RL and MetaClaw-style personal agents.
  - **Researcher direction:** Aligning Autoresearch, PaperClaw.

  Almost all of them sit at L1–L2 of Duan et al.'s ladder (2609.11873, which defines L1 Execution to L5 Meta / "recursive inheritance" ✓). Reglos places itself at L2 (strategy autonomy) for its harness loop and L4 (environment adaptation) for its memory loop ✓ §3.4. In CARE's terms, borrowed from Chen 2607.07663, they are "human-on-the-loop": the loop is automatic, but a person approves promotion (✓ CARE §2.1; Chen ✓).
- **State of the art, production.** CARE (Keeta/Meituan with Melbourne and Fudan, 2611.02839) is the most complete report.
  - Five iterations of failure-attributed on-policy self-distillation took a Gemma-4-31B agent's Bad Case rate from 6.42% to 1.97%, against 4.60% for the GPT-5.4 incumbent ✓.
  - Online satisfaction went from −4.6 pp (p = 0.03) to parity (+1.73 pp, p = 0.47, not significant) ✓.
  - Serving cost per order fell 70.5% ✓.

  LinkedIn's self-evolving support agent (2608.10224) ran a user-randomized two-week A/B test: +9.0 pp QA self-serve and +30.6 pp routing accuracy ✓.
- **State of the art, human feedback as the objective.** In RSI Arena (2610.33624), 10 frontier agents post-trained the same 30B MoE base.
  - The best agent (GPT-6 Astra) closed a median 76% of the base→Instruct gap across 12 capability benchmarks ✓.
  - In Stage 2, after receiving 213–276 human battles each, 8 of 10 narrowed their style-controlled gap to NVIDIA Instruct (median +28 points across all ten) ✓.
  - The benchmark change and the human-rating change were unrelated (ρ = −0.19) ✓.
- **Consensus.**
  1. Humans keep the promotion decision.
  2. The judge or attributor must be independent of the learner.
  3. Updates go through versioned, reversible artifacts with rollback.
  4. Raw user feedback is evidence, not a reward to maximize.

  CARE, LinkedIn, ESCROW, LOGOS, Reglos and Recoverability/Verifier-Strength all converge on this ✓ (ESCROW and LOGOS: abstract and introduction checked in full text).
- **Consensus on the learning signal.** Small increments of production repairs break fixed-target objectives.
  - In CARE, on the same 280 repair tuples, SFT collapsed during training and DPO collapsed into immediate (first-turn) handoff (15.1% simulation accuracy).
  - On-policy self-distillation stayed at 94.1% ✓.
- **The central negative result.** Feedback-driven evolution creates new failure modes that a pre-deployment audit cannot see:
  - Agents learn that length is "the only lever" (RSI Arena ✓ §7).
  - Positive feedback teaches personal agents to execute injected instructions. Attack success rises by 14.0–48.8 pp under skill evolution (2610.39122 ✓).
  - Deployed changes alter 17% of task outcomes beyond the noise floor, which no rollback repairs (2610.27465 ✓ §5).
- **Biggest open problem.** No study we found isolates the causal value of human feedback from the extra compute and time it comes with. A Semantic Scholar and ICLR 2027 OpenReview search for placebo or shuffled-feedback controls found none for human feedback. RSI Arena's Stage 2 has no placebo-vote arm, and the authors say their comparisons "do not isolate the effect of human feedback" ✓ §7. No production system makes the *improver itself* subject to improvement: CARE's retrospection, attribution and repair are run by an external frontier model ✓ §3.3. This corner therefore has, in Duan's terms, effective object-level improvement but no structural recursion.

### Taxonomy

The corner divides along three axes:

1. **Feedback source:** population preference, individual user correction, production failure evidence, or expert direction.
2. **Update locus:** weights, or harness/prompt/skill/memory.
3. **Where the human sits:** in the loop, meaning they judge each update; on the loop, meaning they approve promotion; or only defining the objective.

| Approach | Feedback source → update | Human position | Representative papers |
